documents: A new measurement method for brain scans may help doctors detect early signs of Alzheimer's disease more accurately than standard scans. This method could also help explain how brain damage affects thinking and memory in people with the disease.

Researchers plan to test if this improved scanning method can better distinguish between people with Alzheimer's disease and healthy people. The goal is to make the results of brain scans clearer and more reliable for understanding the disease.
A specialized brain scan method provides a clearer and more accurate picture of the damage to the brain's connecting tissues in people with Alzheimer's disease than standard scans do.
The study shows that standard brain scans can be misled by fluid in the brain, which makes a newer scan type better at revealing the true extent of the disease's impact on brain structure.
The findings indicate that the brain's white matter is significantly affected by Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that measuring this tissue could be a useful way to track the condition.

Scans of the brain's supporting tissue in people with Alzheimer's disease show signs of damage that might appear before memory loss or other symptoms start, suggesting these scans could help detect the disease early.

Some studies found a link between brain scan results and thinking ability in people with Alzheimer's disease, but other studies did not find a clear connection, so it is not yet certain how well these scans predict cognitive function.
The group of people with Alzheimer's disease in this study had significantly lower scores on memory and thinking tests compared to the healthy group, while the two groups were similar in age.

Standard brain scans can be inaccurate in people with Alzheimer's disease because fluid builds up in the brain as tissue is lost, which can make the results reflect a mix of different tissues rather than just the nerve fibers.

A specific method has been developed to remove the effect of this extra fluid from the scan data, which helps make the measurements of the brain's nerve fibers more accurate and specific to the tissue.

Researchers found areas in the brain where people with Alzheimer's disease showed different tissue characteristics compared to healthy people, but these differences were only found in one direction, meaning the disease group had higher values in specific regions. The study did not find evidence of the opposite pattern where healthy people had higher values in those same areas.

The finding that the main nerve bundle connecting the two sides of the brain shows damage in the front and middle sections suggests that brain degeneration may start in the front and move backward, but this pattern is not yet proven.

In areas where nerve bundles cross, the measurement of brain health appears falsely better in people with the disease because the crossing nerves are lost, meaning the actual damage is likely worse than the standard test suggests.

Using a method that removes the influence of extra fluid from brain scans makes the measurements of brain tissue damage more accurate and better matches the expected patterns of disease in people with Alzheimer's disease. The evidence shows this method improves the reliability of the results, but it does not show that the method works for every single patient.

The measurements of how water moves in specific directions within the brain are more easily distorted by extra fluid than the general measure of tissue structure. This means the specific direction measurements are less reliable without a correction step to remove the fluid's effect.

The study found that a specific measurement method for brain health was not linked to how well people with early-stage memory loss performed on a standard mental test. This lack of a connection may be because the participants all had very similar, mild symptoms, making it hard to see differences.

Researchers note that the link between the physical condition of brain tissue and thinking skills is still not fully understood. Using a more precise measurement technique is recommended for future studies to better understand this relationship.

Newer imaging measurements offer a clearer and more precise view of the brain tissue changes linked to Alzheimer's disease. This means the evidence is more confident in identifying the specific damage to the white matter in people affected by the condition.

A new method for analyzing brain scans removes interference from brain shrinkage, making it more accurate at detecting the specific damage caused by Alzheimer's disease. This improved accuracy helps researchers better understand the condition, though it does not yet show how brain changes relate to overall memory scores.

The study found that a new scanning technique is better at identifying the specific brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease compared to standard methods. This means the new technique provides a clearer picture of the disease's impact on the brain's connecting fibers.

Researchers using a standard public brain scan database found that a specific software tool was missing the exact settings needed to reproduce their results, meaning the findings cannot be independently verified by others.

A statistical analysis claiming a strong result is considered unreliable if it fails to show the range of likely outcomes or if it did not adjust for the many tests performed, making the core claim fragile regardless of data quality.

The specific computer code used to calculate the brain damage measurements is not publicly available, which prevents anyone from checking if the reported 'extra damage' is a real biological effect or just a mistake created by the software's default settings.

For people whose memory problems are worsening into Alzheimer's disease, specific changes in how signals travel through certain brain pathways are linked to the loss of thinking skills, while other types of signal changes are not. This evidence suggests that measuring one specific type of signal change in the brain could help doctors spot early signs of cognitive decline and track the disease's progression, though it does not prove that these brain changes cause the memory loss.

The researchers focused on specific measures of brain tissue structure to better understand the distinct changes happening in Alzheimer's disease, rather than using a general measure that mixes different types of damage together.
The method used to analyze the brain scans has a limitation because it only looks at the central core of the brain's wiring, which might miss early signs of damage in the outer or crossing areas.

The detailed examination of specific brain regions was done after the initial broad scan, so these specific results should be interpreted with caution because they were not based on pre-planned predictions.

Early signs of brain damage, such as nerve fiber injury and inflammation, can be detected before symptoms become severe. Finding these changes early is important for starting treatment at the right time to slow down memory loss.

Scientists want to know if measuring brain damage over time can predict how a person's memory will decline. This could help identify people at risk of developing Alzheimer's disease before they show clear symptoms.

The study followed a small group of people who had mild memory problems at the start and developed Alzheimer's disease two years later. Researchers looked at how their brain structure changed during this period to understand the link between brain damage and worsening memory.

The study found that people in the group experienced a significant worsening of their cognitive abilities over a two-year period. The researchers checked to make sure that the people who were left out of the main analysis because of missing data were similar to the people who were included, and they found no major differences between the two groups in terms of age, gender, education, or starting health status.

Changes in the health of a specific nerve pathway in the left side of the brain were linked to how much a person's dementia symptoms worsened, but the evidence for this link is not strong enough to be certain.
The study did not find any clear connection between changes in a different measure of nerve fiber health and the worsening of dementia symptoms in any of the brain areas examined.

The study found that the health of specific nerve pathways in the left and right sides of the brain is strongly linked to how much a person's thinking and memory abilities decline. This means that damage to these specific brain connections is a clear sign of worsening dementia symptoms in the people studied.

The evidence strongly suggests that the condition of the nerve fibers in the left internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus is closely related to the severity of cognitive decline. This finding indicates that monitoring these specific areas could help understand how dementia progresses in individuals.

The study found that the physical condition of the brain's connecting pathways worsened in many areas between the start and the end of the study. This finding applies to the group of people studied, who were older adults with dementia.

The people in this study were older adults who were already showing signs of dementia, and their condition became more severe over time. The study did not find that the worsening of the brain's connecting pathways was linked to the participants' sex, education level, or whether they carried a specific gene associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Damage to specific nerve pathways in the brain, particularly those connected to memory and thinking, is linked to worsening cognitive function in people with the disease. This suggests that the breakdown of these nerve fibers is a key driver of the mental decline experienced by patients.

The study found that the loss of nerve fibers, rather than the damage to their protective coating, is the main factor associated with the progression of cognitive decline in this stage of the illness. This indicates that the early stages of the disease are characterized by the shrinking of nerve structures rather than the loss of their insulation.

The deterioration of nerve fibers in a specific area of the brain is connected to the worsening of mental abilities, confirming that this physical damage contributes to the loss of cognitive skills. While other areas showed some trends toward this link, the connection was not strong enough to be considered certain in those specific locations.

The study found a strong link between damage to the brain's main connecting pathways and worsening memory and thinking skills, but it did not find a similar link for another type of tissue damage. The evidence is considered highly reliable for this specific connection.

Damage to the brain's central bridge, which connects the left and right sides, can weaken memory, attention, and language skills because it disrupts the smooth flow of information between the two halves of the brain. The study suggests that injury to these specific pathways leads to noticeable declines in daily functioning and cognitive abilities.

Previous research confirms that the structural changes in the brain's connecting pathways seen in this study are consistent with earlier findings in people with Alzheimer's disease. These changes are associated with lower scores on standard mental health tests, supporting the idea that this brain damage is a key part of the disease's progression.

Damage to the nerve fibers in the brain is a main cause of memory loss and thinking problems in people with Alzheimer's disease, while damage to the protective coating of these fibers is less important. This means that measuring how well the nerve fibers are holding together could help doctors spot the early stages of the disease before severe symptoms appear.

Tracking how the nerve fibers in the brain change over time gives a clearer picture of how the disease progresses than taking a single snapshot, which could help in diagnosing the condition early. However, this method is not yet ready for routine use because different hospitals use different equipment and there are no standard rules for what results are considered abnormal.

The study had a small number of participants, so the results might not apply to everyone, and the tools used to measure thinking skills were not detailed enough to show exactly which mental abilities were failing. This means the findings need to be confirmed in larger groups of people using more thorough tests of memory and attention to be sure they are reliable.

The research suggests that a specific type of brain scan measurement could serve as an early warning sign for the progression of Alzheimer's disease, helping to detect changes before they become severe. However, the study notes that the sample size was small, so the results are not yet definitive and require further testing with more people to be certain.

Because the study included only a small number of people with very mild symptoms, the data is too weak to show any meaningful link between the scan results and how the disease affects daily life, so no conclusions can be drawn about how this tool will help patients.

A study involving a small group of people with Alzheimer's disease and healthy individuals found that detailed brain scans can reveal specific changes in the brain's internal structure that are linked to how well a person thinks and remembers. The researchers were moderately confident that these specific scan details are useful for understanding the condition, but the study does not prove that these scans can be used as a standalone test to diagnose the disease.
The study involved people with mild memory problems or dementia, along with healthy people, who all agreed to participate and underwent detailed thinking tests.
People were excluded from the study if they had severe blood vessel problems in the brain, serious psychiatric history, or if they were left-handed.
All participants had their brains scanned using a specific type of magnetic imaging machine that took about ten minutes to complete.

Alzheimer's disease is a major global health issue that causes a gradual loss of memory and thinking skills, eventually leading to a complete loss of independence. The condition is the leading cause of dementia, affecting the vast majority of people with this diagnosis.

The physical damage in the brain that causes memory loss happens before the brain shrinks in size. This means that finding early signs of this specific damage is crucial for understanding how the disease affects a person's daily life.

A common brain scan used to study Alzheimer's disease has a known weakness because it assumes water moves in a simple, predictable way. This assumption makes the scan less effective at detecting the complex, uneven changes happening in the brain tissue.

A newer type of brain scan is becoming more popular because it overcomes the limitations of the older scan method. It works by looking at specific parts of the brain's structure in more detail, which helps researchers better understand the physical changes associated with the disease.

The study compared brain tissue structure in people with Alzheimer's disease to healthy people to find differences, but the methods used are too technical to explain what this means for patients in plain language.
Researchers looked for links between how well people think and their brain scan results, but the specific findings and confidence levels are not described in simple terms.

In people with Alzheimer's disease, the strength of certain brain connections is linked to how well they perform on memory and thinking tests. This connection was strongest in specific areas of the brain, suggesting that damage to these pathways is associated with cognitive decline.

The evidence strongly supports that changes in specific brain regions are related to cognitive scores in Alzheimer's disease patients. However, the study only selected a few brain areas for display and does not show that these changes cause the cognitive decline.

New brain scan methods show that damage to the brain's wiring in people with Alzheimer's disease is more widespread than previously thought. These scans can help identify the disease and reflect how well a person's thinking and memory are working.

The evidence strongly supports that these specific brain scan measures are useful for detecting the brain changes linked to Alzheimer's disease. However, the study does not prove that these scans can predict future memory loss or cure the disease.

The strength of brain cell connections in specific areas is closely linked to how well people with Alzheimer's disease perform on thinking tests, meaning that better connections suggest better mental function. The evidence for this link is very strong.
Some measures of brain cell structure are strongly connected to mental test scores, but other measures of the space around cells showed no clear link to how well people perform on these tests.
A specific type of brain scan measure can help distinguish between people with Alzheimer's disease and those with mild memory problems, showing a high level of accuracy in identifying the condition.

Advanced brain scans can detect tiny physical changes in the brain that are linked to memory loss and cognitive decline, helping to identify the disease in its early stages. The evidence suggests these scans are useful for spotting these changes, but they do not show every possible aspect of the disease.

Brain scans show that the inside of nerve cells shrinks and the space between them grows larger in people with the disease, which is caused by the buildup of harmful proteins. These physical changes disrupt the normal structure of the nerves, but the scans do not prove that these changes are the sole cause of the symptoms.

Different types of brain scans reveal different aspects of the damage to the brain's wiring, such as the loss of nerve endings or the breakdown of the protective coating around nerves. While these scans show that the brain's structure is changing, they do not fully explain how these changes lead to the specific symptoms experienced by patients.

The brain changes seen in Alzheimer's disease are more widespread than previously thought, extending to areas that control movement and balance, which helps explain the full range of symptoms people experience.
Measures of how water moves through brain tissue are strongly linked to how well a person thinks and remembers, showing that physical damage to the brain's wiring directly causes cognitive decline.
One specific type of brain scan measurement was better at predicting memory and thinking ability than other standard scans, suggesting it is more sensitive to the damage caused by the disease.
Different scanning methods show similar accuracy in detecting the disease, but each provides unique information about the brain's structure that helps build a complete picture of the damage.

The study could not confirm the presence of specific brain proteins in the participants because it did not include the specific brain scans or tissue tests needed for that verification. This means the findings cannot be considered certain proof of the disease's physical cause in these individuals.

The results may not apply to all people with the condition because the group of patients was too small to separate them into different types of the disease. This limits how widely the findings can be used to understand the condition in general.

The study did not account for common age-related changes in the brain's white matter that many older people have. Because of this, it is possible that these common changes influenced the results rather than the disease itself.

The different brain scanning methods used in the study are all useful for looking at how the brain's tiny structures change in people with Alzheimer's disease. Each method provides different useful information about these changes.

It is impossible for anyone to check if these results are real because the researchers did not share the original data or the specific tools they used to analyze it. This lack of transparency means we cannot distinguish a true medical finding from a mistake in the computer analysis.

The claim that a specific brain scan adjustment improves the accuracy of results is currently theoretical because the underlying data was too small and lacked the necessary statistical details to confirm the improvement is real. This means the adjustment should be viewed as a potential refinement for future research, not a proven method for making clinical decisions about patients.

The field has not reached a consensus on the best way to detect early brain changes, with different studies using conflicting methods that may miss specific tissue damage. A definitive answer requires a large study across multiple hospitals with fully open data to verify if the new methods are consistently better than the standard ones.

One study provides its data publicly, which is a positive step, but another key study does not share its code or detailed logs, which prevents independent experts from verifying its results. To settle the debate, we need a large study where all raw data and software versions are open for anyone to test both methods side-by-side.

documents: The study data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls (HC) and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease participants.
The study compared standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics with advanced free-water DTI (FW-DTI) model metrics to assess white matter integrity in the context of Alzheimer's disease.
The study included 30 healthy control participants (17 females, mean age 73 ± 6) and 28 Alzheimer's disease participants (15 females, mean age 75 ± 7).
The Alzheimer's disease cohort was stratified by Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, consisting of 16 participants with CDR 0.5, 10 with CDR 1, 1 with CDR 2, and 1 with CDR 3.
The study utilized diffusion-based magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) analyzed with the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model to evaluate white matter integrity.
A free water (FW) correction algorithm was applied to the DTI data to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular free water, addressing partial volume effects caused by neuronal loss.

The study compared fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean diffusivity (MA) derived from both standard DTI and FW-DTI between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) subjects.
The data for the comparison between AD and HC subjects were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project.
The study analyzed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics from standard DTI and FW-DTI and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score in both AD and HC groups.

The study included 30 healthy controls (17 females; age 73 ± 6 years) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females; age 75 ± 7 years), selected from the OASIS-3 brain project based on ages 60-90 years and the availability of 3 T dMRI data with more than 30 directions.

All diffusion MRI data were acquired using a 3 T Siemens scanner with 64 diffusion-encoding directions, a b value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, a flip-angle of 90°, a matrix of 96×96, a field of view of 24.0 × 24.0 cm, a slice thickness of 2.5 mm, 64 axial slices, and one non-diffusion-weighted B0 image.

The dMRI data were preprocessed using the FMRIB software library tool (FSL, version 5.0.4) to correct for eddy currents and motion, and the brain mask was defined using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) for the single B0 images.
DTI standard and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script, with the FW maps computed by fitting a specific model at each voxel.
Fractional anisotropy (FA) maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script, which is available upon request.
The free-water (FW) maps were computed by fitting a model at each voxel where the b-value was 1000 s/mm² and the water diffusion coefficient (D_water) was set to 3 × 10⁻³ mm²/s.
The mode of anisotropy (MA) was calculated using a formula involving the DTI eigenvalues (λ₁, λ₂, λ₃) to discriminate between linear and planar anisotropy.

The B0 images from each subject were processed using buildtemplateparallel.sh in ANTs to create a B0 groupwise template image, which was then normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image using the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm. The resulting warp fields were applied to transfer all DTI maps to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas (v.4.1) in ICBM-152 space.
All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 3 mm.

Comparisons of DTI and FW-DTI metrics between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and a Family-Wise Error (FWE) correction at a 0.01 level, with the number of randomized permutations set at 5,000. A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and applied to the other DTI maps.

For each voxel, the DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) model that included age and sex as covariates. Statistically different clusters were labeled according to the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) DTI-based white-matter atlases.

The voxel-based relationship between MMSE scores and DTI metrics for the cognitively impaired group was assessed using FSL Randomise with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).

The study used standard DTI metrics, including fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD), to analyze differences between healthy controls (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups. The analysis identified specific brain regions such as the fornix, corpus callosum (CC), right anterior thalamic radiation, cortical spinal tract, posterior limb of internal capsule, and superior corona radiata where significant metric differences were observed.

The statistical analysis for the DTI clusters was performed using ANCOVA with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE). The results were visualized using violin plots representing the DTI metrics inside the significant clusters for each group.

The study applied a False Discovery Rate (FWE) correction threshold of p<0.01 for the Free-Water Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FW-DTI) metrics FA_t, AxD_t, and RD_t, with one exception for a cluster in the corpus callosum which used a p<0.05 FWE corrected threshold.

The analysis compared standard Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) metrics with Free-Water Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FW-DTI) metrics, noting that FW-DTI identified smaller significant clusters in the fornix and corpus callosum compared to standard FA.
The study compared mean anisotropy (MA) values between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups using both standard DTI and FW-DTI analysis methods.
The statistical analysis identified significant differences between groups for FW maps at a p-value threshold of less than 0.01, corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).

The ANCOVA analysis between healthy control and Alzheimer's disease subjects for the mean anisotropy index was performed on both standard DTI and FW-DTI data with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE.

The study compared groups using the FW index at a significance threshold of p<0.01 with False Discovery Rate (FWE) correction, identifying clusters where Alzheimer's Disease (AD) values were higher than Healthy Control (HC) values.

The study reported significant differences between groups at p<0.01 (FWE corrected), except for the RD (HC) < RD (AD) comparison which was reported at p<0.05 (FWE corrected), using the JHU white-matter tractography atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas to define brain areas.

The study used an ANCOVA analysis to compare healthy controls (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects, reporting clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE), with the exception of the radial diffusivity (RDt) comparison which was reported at p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected.

The ANCOVA analysis of the fiber-wise (FW) index between healthy controls and Alzheimer's disease subjects reported clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).
The analysis of the mean anisotropy (MA) index utilized both standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and fiber-wise DTI (FW-DTI) methods, yielding similar results for group-wise significant clusters.
White matter integrity was assessed in patients with Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls using both standard and free water-corrected diffusion tensor imaging metrics.

To mitigate partial volume effects, free water-contaminated voxels were removed by incorporating a free water component into the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline, which produced free water-corrected DTI metrics and a complementary free water index.

The study used a voxel-based correlation analysis with a significance threshold of p < 0.05 corrected for Family-wise Error (FWE) to assess the relationship between MMSE scores and DTI/FW-DTI metrics.

The study reported correlations between FA and AxD, and FA and RD, for both standard and FW-corrected metrics, noting that correlations increased after FW correction (e.g., FA and AxD correlation in the AD group increased from 0.160 to 0.856).

The study applied fractional anisotropy (FA) correction for free water (FW) to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data to improve the accuracy and sensitivity of the resulting DTI metrics in Alzheimer's disease (AD).

The study utilized skeletonized tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to identify FA reductions in the fornix of early-symptomatic individuals and those at high risk for developing Alzheimer's disease.

The study compared standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) with free water diffusion tensor imaging (FW-DTI) to assess changes in the corpus callosum (CC), observing large clusters of lower FA in the genu and body using both methods.

The study employed mean anisotropy (MA) as a metric of diffusion anisotropy to provide insight into areas with crossing fibers where standard DTI methods are unable to resolve different fiber orientations within a voxel.

The study analyzed the assumption of Gaussian diffusion implicit in the tensor model of standard DTI, noting that this limitation causes FA to be artificially diminished in the presence of crossing fibers.

The study utilized a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach like TBSS, a methodological choice that increases the number of available voxels and sensitivity to subtle microstructural differences but is inherently more sensitive to partial volume effects.

The white matter analysis relied on atlases that covered only 84% of the white matter mask, a limitation that is particularly relevant for the FW index which showed widespread changes across white matter regions outside the atlas coverage.
The study applied a voxel-based correlation threshold of p<0.01 with FWE correction, which yielded no significant correlations between standard DTI and FW-DTI metrics and the MMSE score.

The study utilized Free Water (FW) correction algorithms to process Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data, distinguishing between standard DTI metrics and Free Water-corrected metrics (FW-AxD_t, FW-RD_t, and FW-FA_t).

The Free Water volume fraction was quantified using the FW-correction algorithm, with specific regional percentages reported for structures such as the cingulum (85.16% and 56.34%), ILF and IFOF (52% and 40%), forceps major and minor (approximately 40% each), ATR (31.39%), fornix (95.6%), and corpus callosum (approximately 56%).

The study did not observe significant voxel-wise correlations between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and DTI metrics before or after Free Water correction, a limitation attributed to the cohort's predominantly very mild to mild Alzheimer's Disease status and the narrow range of MMSE scores.
The study utilized the OASIS brain database, which provides longitudinal MRI data for nondemented and demented older adults.
The analysis employed the FSL software suite for functional and structural MR image analysis.
The study applied an integrated approach to correct for off-resonance effects and subject movement in diffusion MR imaging.
The study utilized fast robust automated brain extraction for image processing.
The study employed symmetric diffeomorphic image registration with cross-correlation for automated labeling.
The study used a high angular resolution diffusion imaging human brain template for spatial standardization.
The statistical analysis utilized permutation inference for the general linear model.
The study applied threshold-free cluster enhancement to address problems of smoothing, threshold dependence, and localization in cluster inference.
The study used tract probability maps in stereotaxic spaces for white matter anatomy analysis and tract-specific quantification.
The study assessed the reproducibility of quantitative tractography methods applied to cerebral white matter.
The study utilized the Mini-mental state exam as a practical method for grading the cognitive state of patients.

The study selected eighteen participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment at baseline and Alzheimer's disease at follow-up from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative for a 2-year longitudinal analysis.
Tract-based spatial statistics was used to assess longitudinal changes in white matter, with statistical models controlling for age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status.
Voxel-wise and region-of-interest analyses were conducted to examine the association between axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity changes and changes in clinical dementia rating scores.

The study utilizes diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to detect microstructural changes and white matter tract integrity, relying on the principle that water diffusion aligns with fiber orientation and that damage reduces anisotropy.

The study employs axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) as DTI metrics, where AxD represents the rate of water diffusion along the longitudinal axis (principal eigenvector λ1) and RD reflects the rate of water diffusion along the perpendicular axes.

The methodological choice to use AxD and RD is based on their ability to detect distinct pathological mechanisms, with AxD detecting axonal degeneration and RD detecting changes related to demyelination.
The study utilized data sourced from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database on 14 February 2024, with the authors having no access to participant-identifying information.

Participants were selected from the ADNI cohort who underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), cognitive assessments, and demographic evaluations at baseline and a 2-year follow-up, with follow-up assessments conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after the baseline assessment.

The final analysis included 18 participants (age 72.00 ± 8.69 years; 6 [33.33%] females) who were diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline and progressed to Alzheimer's disease (AD) at the follow-up examination, while 44 participants with missing baseline or follow-up DTI images were excluded.
The longitudinal changes in axonal damage (AxD) and radial diffusion (RD) were evaluated using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented with the FMRIB Software Library (FSL).

The study used FSL version 6.0.6 to register fractional anisotropy maps to a custom FMRIB58_FA 1 x 1 x 1 mm template space created from the 18 participants in the study. A mean fractional anisotropy skeleton was constructed by averaging the maps, and a threshold of 0.2 was applied to refine the skeleton to include only voxels with sufficient fractional anisotropy values.

The Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas was used to apply region-of-interest masks to the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus to extract axial and radial diffusivity values. These region-of-interest analyses were conducted in an exploratory, post hoc manner based on regions showing significant differences in the whole-brain analysis, rather than based on a priori hypotheses.

All statistical analyses were conducted using Jamovi version 2.3.28.0 and FSL version 6.0.6. Longitudinal differences in axial and radial diffusivity values were analyzed using Tract-Based Spatial Statistics with permutation-based statistical testing.

Permutation testing with 5,000 iterations generated a null distribution of t-values by randomly rearranging the data among the participants to evaluate group variations and avoid arbitrary spatial smoothing. A threshold-free cluster enhancement method was applied within the permutation-based paired t-tests to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level, with statistical significance set at P < 0.05.

A general linear model was incorporated into the Tract-Based Spatial Statistics framework to account for potential confounding factors, with age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status as independent variables and axial or radial diffusivity as the dependent variable.

The final analysis included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female. Participants with at least one apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele were classified as carriers, while those with no APOE ε4 alleles were classified as non-carriers.
The requirement for written informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board of Gachon University (approval number 1044396-202405-HR-086-01).

Dementia severity was assessed using the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), which combines data from patient and caregiver interviews across six cognitive domains. Participants were classified into cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups at both time points based on CDR scores in accordance with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) criteria.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores over the 2-year period, calculated as the CDR at follow-up minus the CDR at baseline.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired for each participant using a 3T MRI scanner, with detailed imaging protocols described in publicly available documents from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI).

FSL version 6.0.6 and MRtrix3 were used to correct DTI artifacts, including noise, Gibbs artifacts, eddy current-induced distortions, and bias field inhomogeneity. The diffusion tensor model was fitted using the "dtifit" tool in FSL to generate eigenvalue maps λ1, λ2, and λ3.
Axial diffusivity (AxD) was determined using the primary eigenvalue (λ1), while radial diffusivity (RD) was derived by averaging the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3).

A general linear model was incorporated into the Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) framework with age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and axial diffusivity (AxD) or radial diffusivity (RD) as the dependent variable. Spearman's correlation analysis examined changes in region-of-interest (ROI)-based AxD, RD, and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) in specific white matter regions while controlling for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score.

Uncorrected P-values were reported for correlation analyses because applying the Bonferroni correction would have significantly lowered statistical power due to the small sample size. A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate the adequacy of the sample size in detecting meaningful correlations.

Multiple linear regression analysis evaluated the independent contributions of axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) changes to clinical development, with the change in Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables. Age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score were treated as confounders in the regression model, which was conducted independently for each white matter region showing notable variations in AxD or RD in the Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis.

Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the included group (n=18) and the excluded group (n=44) to assess potential sample bias due to the exclusion of participants with missing diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data. No significant differences were found between the included and excluded groups in age (P=0.909), sex (P=0.578), education level (P=0.967), APOE ε4 carrier status (P=0.251), and baseline Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) (P=0.074).

The study utilized tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to analyze white matter changes, identifying significant alterations in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) at baseline and follow-up.

Statistical significance for the decreased diffusivity metrics (AxD and RD) was determined using a threshold of P<0.05 after correcting for multiple comparisons with the family-wise error (FWE) method.
Table 2 reports the specific voxel sizes for significant changes in AxD and RD across white matter regions, such as 1625 voxels for AxD and 1387 voxels for RD in the splenium of the corpus callosum.
The study participants consisted of 18 individuals (6 female, 12 male) with a mean baseline age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69) and a mean baseline Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) of 2.42 (SD 1.17).
APOE ε4 carrier status was defined such that participants with one or more APOE ε4 alleles were classified as carriers, while those with no APOE ε4 alleles were classified as non-carriers.
Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis was used to evaluate white matter integrity changes between baseline and follow-up examinations.
The study longitudinally evaluated white matter microstructure changes by analyzing diffusion metrics AxD and RD, which are anisotropic diffusion metrics measured using DTI.
The study assessed the associations between white matter microstructure changes and cognitive decline using regression analysis, with results summarized in S2 Table.
The study utilized TBSS analysis to identify significant changes in AxD and RD across the CC, CR, CG, SLF, IFOF, and IC.

The study conducted a post hoc power analysis using G*Power version 3.1, which indicated 93.7% power to detect a correlation of r=0.704 and 86.3% power for the average observed correlation (mean r=0.644) with alpha=0.05 and N=18.

The analysis of white matter integrity and clinical dementia rating changes utilized multiple linear regression with CDR changes as the dependent variable, adjusting for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR.

The regression analysis specifically involved regions of interest that exhibited significant differences in both axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity values in the tract-based spatial statistics analysis.
The scatter plots displayed residualized axial diffusivity and clinical dementia rating change values after adjusting for age, sex, education, APOE epsilon 4 status, and baseline CDR.

The study used a correlation analysis to assess associations between white matter integrity metrics (axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity) and cognitive decline measured by the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score.

The analysis identified significant correlations between axial diffusivity changes and CDR score changes in specific white matter regions, including the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (r=0.704, P=0.007), left posterior corona radiata (r=0.676, P=0.011), left fornix cres stria terminalis (r=0.627, P=0.022), and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (r=0.568, P=0.043).

Table 3 presents the specific correlation coefficients (r) and P-values for the relationship between axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity in various white matter regions and Clinical Dementia Rating scores.

The study utilized multivariate regression analysis to investigate the separate effects of AxD and RD changes on clinical progression. The analysis identified that AxD changes in the left retrolenticular IC correlated with CDR changes.
The study was a longitudinal study examining the progression from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's disease (AD).
The study used diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics, specifically axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), to assess white matter microstructural changes.
The analysis involved a multivariate regression analysis of AxD and RD changes on Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score changes.

The study employed a longitudinal design to analyze the progression from Mild Cognitive Impairment to Alzheimer's Disease, evaluating microstructural changes in white matter integrity to assess subtle pathological changes over time.
The study utilized a small sample size of n=18 participants, which limits the generalizability of the findings and reduces statistical power, increasing the likelihood of overlooking subtle changes.

The study reported uncorrected p-values due to the small sample size, acknowledging the risk of inflated false-positive rates, and notes that future validation requires more stringent correction methods such as False Discovery Rate.

The Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis focused exclusively on the core regions of the white matter tract by projecting the highest fractional anisotropy values onto the alignment-invariant tract representation (the FA skeleton), which may overlook subtle changes occurring outside the skeleton.

Cognitive function was evaluated using Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores only, which lacks a detailed assessment of various cognitive domains and does not capture domain-specific cognitive deficits.

Region of interest (ROI) analyses were conducted post hoc based on Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) findings, which may raise concerns about circular reasoning and requires future validation using a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets.

APOE ε4 status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, but potential interaction effects between ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested due to the limited sample size and small number of ε4 carriers.
The study by Takahashi et al. (2002) measured selective reduction of diffusion anisotropy in the white matter of Alzheimer disease brains using 3.0 Tesla magnetic resonance imaging.

The study by Lai et al. (2024) utilized a cross-sectional case-control design to investigate structural changes in brain white matter tracts associated with overactive bladder using diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging.
The study by Bergamino et al. (2021) employed free-water diffusion tensor imaging to improve the accuracy and sensitivity of white matter analysis in Alzheimer's disease.
The study by Saito et al. (2023) assessed the reproducibility of an automated calculation technique for diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space.
The study by Shu et al. (2011) utilized a tract-based spatial statistics approach to reveal white matter degeneration in Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.
The study by Qi et al. (2024) employed a cross-sectional design using both tract-based spatial statistics and fixel-based analysis to assess cerebral white matter injury in haemodialysis patients.

The study by Li et al. (2024) applied the tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) method to analyze diffusion kurtosis imaging data regarding brain white matter alteration in patients with coronary artery disease.
The study by Allen et al. (2019) stratified patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment using advanced diffusion metrics and neurocognitive testing.
The study by Liu et al. (2020) utilized a DTI study using TBSS analysis to examine micro-structural white matter abnormalities and cognitive impairment in asymptomatic carotid plaque patients.
The study by Stahl et al. (2007) assessed white matter damage in Alzheimer disease and mild cognitive impairment using diffusion-tensor MR imaging and parallel imaging techniques.
The study by Reijmer et al. (2012) utilized spherical deconvolution based tractography to improve sensitivity to cerebral white matter abnormalities in Alzheimer's disease.
The study by Kincses et al. (2013) identified patterns of diffusion parameter changes in Alzheimer's Disease using Linked Independent Component Analysis.

The study's reproducibility is critically compromised because the in-house MATLAB script for voxel-wise fitting is only available 'upon request,' and the specific `b`-value matrix used for acquisition is not provided, preventing independent verification of whether the reported 'extra damage' is an artifact of the fitting algorithm's default parameters.

The validity of the free-water model's sensitivity is threatened by the unvalidated assumption of a fixed D_water coefficient, which may inflate the free-water fraction and amplify noise rather than reveal true pathology, a risk that cannot be ruled out without explicit validation of this parameter against the specific acquisition protocol.

The statistical analysis exhibits inconsistent multiple-comparison handling, using a p < 0.01 FWE-corrected threshold for FA and MD in the fornix but a less stringent p < 0.05 FWE threshold for RD_t, which weakens the claim that the free-water model reveals a new biological signal in the n = 28 cohort.
The study enrolled 43 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls who underwent diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) and conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

The acquired images were processed to obtain diffusion MRI models and multiparameter values, which were then analyzed using Pearson correlation analysis and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.

The study utilizes diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) to sensitize the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signal to water molecule diffusion, with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) serving as the primary model for studying white matter changes.

The diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model assumes that water molecule diffusion in the brain follows a Gaussian distribution, a methodological limitation that weakens the capability to detect diffusion heterogeneity in brain tissue.

Neurite Orientation Density and Dispersion Imaging (NODDI) is a biophysical-based model that characterizes brain changes by assuming the diffusion-weighted imaging signal emanates from three distinct tissue compartments: within neurites, outside of neurites, and free water.

The primary parameters derived from the Neurite Orientation Density and Dispersion Imaging (NODDI) model are intracellular volume fraction (ICVF), extracellular volume fraction (ECVF), isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF), and orientation dispersion index (ODI).
The study combined NODDI, MAP-MRI, and DTI models to investigate AD-related microstructural changes and their association with cognitive function.
The diffusion MRI models were concurrently obtained from diffusion spectral imaging (DSI), a grid acquisition model that reconstructs diverse diffusion MRI models via raw diffusion data.
The study assessed the diagnostic performance of different parameters using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.
The study assessed correlations of diffusion MRI parameter values with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores.

The diffusion MRI acquisition protocol used 24 directions at b=1000 s/mm², 3 directions at b=3000 s/mm², and a total of 128 diffusion samples with a total scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.
Diffusion data analysis was performed using in-house prototype software developed by MR Station (Chengdu Zhongying Medical Technology Co., Ltd.) after converting raw data to NIFTI format.
Preprocessing of the diffusion data involved eddy current correction using FSL and denoising with a Gaussian filter with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 3 mm.
Three diffusion models (DTI, MAP-MRI, and NODDI) were fitted to the processed data to derive quantitative microstructural parameter maps.

The study enrolled 43 patients with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls, with healthy controls required to have no cognitive impairment, an MMSE score of 25 or higher, a MoCA score of 25 or higher, and a CDR score of 0.

Exclusion criteria for all participants included severe cerebrovascular disorder, severe white matter hyperintensity, history of psychiatric illness or severe injury, use of cognition-influencing medications, left-handedness, contraindications to MRI, and poor-quality MRI images due to movement artifacts.

All participants underwent diffusion spectrum imaging on a 3.0T Siemens Skyra MRI scanner equipped with a 32-channel head coil, using an axial plane and half q-space Cartesian grid sampling with a TR/TE of 4400/108 ms, field of view of 220 x 220 mm², SMS factor of 2, slice thickness of 2.0 mm, voxel size of 2.0 x 2.0 x 2.0 mm², and 60 slices.
The diffusion spectrum imaging acquisition used 128 total diffusion sampling directions across b-values ranging from 0 to 3000 s/mm², with a total scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.
The study included 43 Alzheimer's disease patients and 16 healthy volunteers, with the Alzheimer's disease group having a significantly higher average age than the healthy control group.

Statistical analysis used a significance level of p<0.05 and applied false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons, with sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and area under the curve calculated using SPSS software.

Regression models between diffusion parameters and Alzheimer's disease were constructed using multivariate binary logistic regression analysis, adjusted for the square of age, gender, and years of education.
The study included 43 participants in the Alzheimer's disease group and 16 participants in the healthy control group.

The Alzheimer's disease group had a mean age of 72.86 ± 8.23 years and a median education of 9 years, while the healthy control group had a mean age of 65.81 ± 8.50 years and a median education of 11 years.
Neuropsychologic assessments were performed using the mini-mental state examination and the Montreal cognitive assessment, with data for these scores available for 25 Alzheimer's disease patients.
The study utilized diffusion tensor imaging parameters including axial diffusivity, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, and radial diffusivity.
The study utilized NODDI parameters including extracellular volume fraction, intracellular volume fraction, and isotropic volume fraction.

The study utilized MAP-MRI parameters including mean-squared displacement, non-Gaussianity, axial non-Gaussianity, radial non-Gaussianity, q-space inverse variance, return-to-origin probability, return-to-axis probability, and return-to-plane probability.
Statistical significance for the spatial distribution of diffusion parameters was defined as P < 0.001.

The study assessed disparities between patients with Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls using a tract-based spatial statistics pipeline within the FSL toolbox from the Oxford Centre for Functional MRI of the Brain.

Fractional anisotropy maps for Alzheimer's disease and healthy control participants were nonlinearly registered to the FMRIB58_FA template, followed by affine alignment into the 1 x 1 x 1 mm³ Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI152) standard space.
Aligned images were averaged and skeletonized to create a mean fractional anisotropy skeleton, onto which the fractional anisotropy and other diffusion parameter maps of each subject were projected.
The whole brain was separated into 50 brain regions by employing the Johns Hopkins University (JHU)-White Matter-labels as masks.

Nonparametric permutation tests were carried out using the randomize tool with 5000 random permutations, and threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) was utilized for multiple comparison correction with a statistical threshold of p<0.001.
Statistical analyses were conducted using the IBM SPSS 23.0 software package (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA).

Pearson correlation analysis was implemented to assess the relationship between clinical cognitive scores and diffusion parameter values, with a criterion for statistical significance set at p<0.05 and a false discovery rate (FDR) used to correct for multiple comparisons.
The study analyzed 25 Alzheimer's disease patients for correlations between neuropsychological scores and diffusion parameters.
The correlation analyses utilized DTI-derived parameters (AxD, FA, MD, RD), NODDI-derived parameters (ECVF, ICVF, ISOVF), and MAP-MRI-derived parameters (MSD, QIV, NG, NGAx, NGRad, RTAP, RTOP, RTPP).

The diagnostic capabilities of diffusion parameters in six specific brain regions (splenium of the corpus callosum, fornix, cerebral peduncle R/L, anterior corona radiata R, and stria terminalis R) were evaluated using ROC curve analysis for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment.

The study used Delong's test to compare the AUC of MAP-RTOP and NODDI-ECVF, finding a significant difference with a p-value of 0.027. The study utilized DTI, NODDI, and MAP-MRI diffusion models to analyze white matter microstructural changes in Alzheimer's disease patients.

The study utilized a NODDI model that relies on the Watson distribution, a methodological choice that may limit the accuracy of the Orientation Dispersion Index (ODI) in complex regions such as kissing fibers, crossing axons, and areas with diffuse pathological changes.

The study employed Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI), which assumes that the diffusion of water molecules in the brain follows a Gaussian distribution, a methodological limitation that restricts its ability to detect the diffusion heterogeneity of brain tissue.

The study applied MAP-MRI metrics that characterize non-Gaussian diffusion profiles, a methodological approach that reflects more complex tissue organization and may be particularly sensitive to neurodegenerative changes such as axonal degeneration and demyelination.
The study lacked positron emission tomography (PET) examinations or pathologic verification confirming tau protein deposition in participants with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.
The Alzheimer's disease groups were not divided into various subtypes due to the relatively small sample size, limiting the wide applicability of the results.

The study did not consider the presence of white matter hyperintensities (WMH) in the analysis, which may have influenced results due to heterogeneous macrostructural white matter impairments across participants older than 60 years.
The study utilized DeLong's test to evaluate statistical differences in AUC values between DTI-derived RD/MD, NODDI-derived ISOVF/ECVF, and MAP-derived RTOP parameters.
The study compared the performance of MAP-MRI, NODDI, and DTI models, finding that MAP-MRI parameters outperformed NODDI and DTI parameters in their association with cognitive function.
The study correlated diffusion metrics RTOP, RTAP, ICVF, and FA with MMSE and MoCA scores to assess the relationship between white matter changes and cognitive function.

The research involving human subjects was examined and approved by the Ethics Committee of Zigong First People's Hospital under protocol number Ethics(Reseach) No. 36, 2023. The patients and participants provided written consent to participate in the study.

The study utilized a sample size of n = 28 with a restricted MMSE range, which Stats identifies as a critical methodological limitation that prevents distinguishing true biological shifts in FA and MD from methodological artifacts due to wide confidence intervals.

The statistical analysis applied an inconsistent multiple-comparison threshold, using p < 0.05 FWE for the RD_t cluster while maintaining p < 0.01 for other metrics, a methodological choice that Stats argues creates an arbitrary boundary for defining new signals.

Replication is blocked because the code generating the cluster maps is only available 'upon request,' preventing verification of whether the relaxed p < 0.05 FWE threshold for the RD_t cluster was a post-hoc decision or part of the pre-registered protocol.

The longitudinal PLOS ONE study utilized a final sample size of n=18 after excluding 44 participants with missing imaging data, a methodological choice that severely limits the statistical power to detect subtle white matter changes.

The TBSS analysis in the referenced study lacks reported effect sizes, confidence intervals, and explicit handling of multiple comparisons, which prevents the distinction between true biological signals and noise in the single time point, small cohort data.

The diagnostic pipeline's reliability is compromised because the raw DICOM files are missing, rendering the unverified registration and the claim of improved sensitivity unsupported by verifiable evidence.

The validity of the cross-paper generalization is undermined by the unresolved debate regarding whether the ROI masks are correctly aligned with the target tissue, indicating a potential bias in the acquisition or processing parameters.

The longitudinal study's effective sample size of 18 is methodologically insufficient to distinguish true microstructural damage from noise, and the reliance on post-hoc region-of-interest analyses inflates the risk of false positives by introducing circular logic in how the regions were defined.

Reproducing the statistical claims for the Sci Rep papers is currently impossible because the raw diffusion data, code, and software versions are missing, and the 2025 PLOS ONE study lacks the specific acquisition parameters and statistical code required to verify the results.

The PLOS ONE study's lack of multiple-comparison correction combined with a sample size of n=18 creates a high risk that reported significant findings are statistical artifacts rather than true biological effects, specifically failing to distinguish specific Alzheimer's signals from general age-related atrophy.

The primary analysis in the discussed studies relies on circular ROI selection, a methodological choice that introduces bias and prevents the verification of whether the claimed pre-neuronal loss damage is distinct from comorbid vascular pathology or general aging.

A definitive study to resolve metric consensus requires a large, multi-site cohort using both standard and free-water corrected models with fully open code and raw data. This design is necessary to verify if corrected metrics consistently outperform standard ones across independent labs, addressing the current lack of consensus on optimal microstructural damage detection.

The 2025 PLOS ONE paper states that all relevant data are in the manuscript and Supporting Information, but it lacks the specific code repository, software versions, and raw data logs needed to independently verify the Family-Wise Error (FWE) thresholds. To replicate the significance boundaries, the exact script generating the uncorrected p-values and the specific b-value schedules are required.

The study with n=18 explicitly states that Bonferroni correction would have eliminated all significant associations, indicating that the reported correlations are artifacts of ignoring the multiple testing problem rather than valid evidence of white matter changes tracking clinical progression. This methodological choice renders the statistical power insufficient to support claims about specific cognitive domains.

documents: The study data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease participants.

The study compared fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean anisotropy (MA) derived from standard DTI and FW-DTI between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) subjects.
The data used for the comparison was obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project.
The study analyzed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics from DTI and FW-DTI and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score.

The study cohort consists of 30 healthy controls (17 female, age 73 ± 6, MMSE 29.10 ± 1.24, CDR 0) and 28 Alzheimer's disease patients (15 female, age 75 ± 7, MMSE 24.18 ± 5.02, CDR 0.82 ± 0.55), with AD patients distributed across CDR scores of 0.5 (n=16), 1 (n=10), 2 (n=1), and 3 (n=1).

The diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model is used to derive fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD) from diffusion-based magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) data to assess white matter integrity.

A free water (FW) correction algorithm is applied to DTI-derived metrics to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular free water, addressing partial volume effects and improving tissue specificity.

FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script that is available upon request. The FW maps were computed by fitting the model A_g(D, f) = f * (exp[-b g^T D g]) + (1-f) * exp[-b D_water] at each voxel.

In the FW model, the b-value is 1000 s/mm^2 and the diffusion coefficient D_water is set to 3 x 10^-3 mm^2/s. Standard DTI metrics are reported as AxD, RD, and FA, while FW-corrected DTI metrics are reported as AxD_t, RD_t, and FA_t.

The mode of anisotropy (MA) is calculated using the DTI eigenvalues (lambda_1, lambda_2, lambda_3) with the formula MA = [(-lambda_1 - lambda_2 + 2lambda_3)(2lambda_1 - lambda_2 - lambda_3)(-lambda_1 + 2lambda_2 - lambda_3)] / [2(lambda_1^2 + lambda_2^2 + lambda_3^2 - lambda_1lambda_2 - lambda_1lambda_3 - lambda_2lambda_3)^(3/2)].

The study used dMRI data from the OASIS-3 brain project (http://oasis-brains.org/), which is freely available, with inclusion criteria of participants aged 60-90 years having 3 T dMRI data with more than 30 directions.

The final cohort included 30 healthy controls (17 females, mean age 73 years) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females, mean age 75 years), with MMSE means of 29.10 for healthy controls and 24.18 for Alzheimer's disease subjects.

All dMRI data were acquired on a Siemens 3 T scanner using 64 diffusion-encoding directions with a b-value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, flip-angle of 90°, matrix of 96×96, field of view of 24.0×24.0 cm, slice thickness of 2.5 mm, and 64 axial slices, plus one non-diffusion-weighted B0 image.

Data preprocessing was performed using the FMRIB software library (FSL, version 5.0.4) for eddy current and motion correction, and the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) for brain masking of single B0 images.
FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script that is available upon request, which is a gap for full replication without direct access to the authors.
The statistical analysis for the standard DTI metrics used an ANCOVA significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
B0 group-wise template images were created using the buildtemplateparallel.sh script in ANTs and normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image using the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm.
DTI maps were transferred to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas version 4.1, which uses International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space.
All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel having a sigma of 3 mm.
Group comparisons of DTI and FW-DTI metrics were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and Family-Wise Error (FWE) correction at a 0.01 level.
A white matter mask was defined by applying a threshold of 0.2 to the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI.
DTI-derived metrics were fitted using an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) model that included age and sex as covariates.
The number of randomized permutations for the statistical analysis was set to 5,000.
Statistically significant clusters were labeled according to the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) DTI-based white-matter atlases.

The voxel-based relationship between Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores and DTI metrics for the Alzheimer's disease group was assessed using FSL Randomise with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).
The study reports specific cluster sizes as a percentage of volume for each brain region in Table 2, and provides corresponding mean DTI values inside significant clusters in Supplementary Table 2.
FW-DTI metrics FA_t, AxD_t, and RD_t were analyzed at a threshold of p<0.01 FWE corrected, with specific cluster coverage percentages reported for the fornix (71%) and corpus callosum (19.2%).
A small cluster inside the body of the corpus callosum showed higher RD_t in the AD group at a threshold of p<0.05 FWE corrected.
Supplementary Table 3 contains the corresponding mean FW-DTI values inside each significant cluster for regions with higher and lower values for each group.

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas defines CC as corpus callosum, LIC as limb of internal capsule, IC as internal capsule, CR as corona radiate, SS as sagittal stratum, and SFOF as superior fronto-occipital fasciculus.

Figure 2 reports ANCOVA analysis clusters between HC and AD subjects for FW-DTI metrics at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE, except for RD_t (HC) < RD_t (AD) which is reported at p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected.

Figure 3 reports ANCOVA analysis clusters between HC and AD subjects for the FW index at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE, with significant clusters covering 34% of the total WM mask.
Significant differences in the FW index between HC and AD subjects were observed in the fornix, cingulum (both hippocampal and cingulate gyrus parts), and corpus callosum (CC).

Significantly higher MA values in AD compared with HC were observed in the right CST, right PLIC, right SCR, and right SFOF, while lower MA values were found in the genu of CC and the external capsule (EC).
Similar results for the MA index were obtained with both standard DTI and FW-DTI analysis, with the complete list of group-wise significant clusters reported in Table 4.

The statistical significance threshold for the Free-water DTI (FW-DTI) analysis was set at p < 0.01 with Family-wise Error (FWE) correction, except for the specific comparison of radial diffusivity (RD) where healthy controls (HC) are lower than Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, which used a threshold of p < 0.05 (FWE corrected).
The study utilized two specific white-matter atlases for region-of-interest analysis: the JHU white-matter tractography atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas.

The JHU white-matter tractography atlas abbreviations used in the data include ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), CGC (cingulum cingulate gyrus part), CGH (cingulum hippocampal part), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus).

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas abbreviations used in the data include CC (corpus callosum), LIC (limb of internal capsule), IC (internal capsule), CR (corona radiate), SS (sagittal stratum), and SFOF (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus).
The study utilized the JHU WM tract atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas to define brain regions for fractional anisotropy analysis.
Fractional anisotropy maps were analyzed using ANCOVA with a significance threshold of p < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
The analysis compared mean anisotropy indices between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects using both standard DTI and FW-DTI methods.
The study incorporated a free water (FW) component into the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline (reference 18) to remove free water-contaminated voxels and produce FW-corrected DTI metrics.

FW correction was applied to DTI metrics in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) subjects to improve accuracy and sensitivity, specifically addressing partial volume effects (PVEs) caused by the proximity of the fornix to the lateral ventricles and atrophy-related ventricular expansion.

Standard DTI methods rely on the assumption of Gaussian diffusion within a tensor model, which creates a gap in replication by failing to resolve different fiber orientations within a single voxel, leading to artificially diminished FA in regions with crossing fibers.
Mean Apparent Diffusivity (MA) was used as a metric of diffusion anisotropy to provide insight in areas of crossing fibers where standard FA is confounded by multi-directional fiber tracts.

The Free Water (FW) volume fraction was quantified using the FW-correction algorithm, with specific cluster percentages reported for the cingulum (85.16% hippocampal, 56.34% cingulate gyrus), ILF (52%), IFOF (40%), forceps major and minor (approximately 40% each), ATR (31.39%), fornix (95.6%), and CC (approximately 56% of total).
Approximately 42% of the Free Water (FW) clusters were located in white matter outside the regions specified by the atlases, with specific increases found in regions bordering various sulcal fundi.

No significant voxel-wise correlations were observed between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) metrics before or after Free Water (FW) correction in the Alzheimer's Disease (AD) cohort, a gap potentially attributable to the narrow range of MMSE scores and the predominantly very mild to mild AD status of the participants.
The study utilized a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach like TBSS, and the atlases used covered 84% of the white matter mask.
The statistical analysis for voxel-based correlations required a p-value threshold of <0.01 with FWE correction.
The MA index analysis identified significant clusters at a threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).

The JHU white-matter tractography atlas abbreviations are defined as ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus).

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas abbreviations are defined as CC (corpus callosum), LIC (limb of internal capsule), CR (corona radiata), EC (external capsule), and SFOF (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus).
No significant voxel-based correlation was found between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and either standard or FW-DTI metrics at the p<0.05 FWE corrected level.
Supplementary Fig. 1 provides population scatter-plots for standard and FW-DTI metrics, including group-wise correlations for Healthy Control (HC) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) groups.
For the Alzheimer's Disease (AD) group, the correlation between Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Axial Diffusivity (AxD) increased from 0.160 (standard) to 0.856 (FW-corrected).
For the Alzheimer's Disease (AD) group, the correlation between Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) changed from -0.464 (standard) to -0.803 (FW-corrected).

The data for the study was provided by the OASIS project, which is supported by NIH Grants P50 AG05681, P01 AG03991, R01 AG021910, P50 MH071616, U24 RR021382, and R01 MH56584.
Supplementary material for the article is available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-86505-7.
