The primary analysis is statistically fragile if it reports p-values without 95% confidence intervals or omits multiple comparisons correction, and replication requires identifying the specific statistical tests used and verifying if the sample size was sufficient to detect the claimed effect size.

The study's generalizability is blocked by a sample size of only 28 patients and a single time point, which prevents the exclusion of methodological artifacts from the free-water model and requires longitudinal data or a larger cohort to distinguish true biological differences from noise.
All relevant data for the study are contained within the manuscript and its Supporting Information files.

The study selected 18 participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline and Alzheimer's disease (AD) at the follow-up examination from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative for a 2-year longitudinal analysis.
Statistical models in the analysis controlled for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status.

The study utilized data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database (adni.loni.usc.edu) accessed on 14 February 2024. The analysis required diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), cognitive assessments, and demographic evaluations at baseline and a 2-year follow-up, with follow-up assessments conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after baseline.

The final analysis included 18 participants (age 72.00 ± 8.69; 6 [33.33%] females) diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline who progressed to Alzheimer's disease (AD) at follow-up. Participants with missing baseline or follow-up DTI images were excluded, resulting in 44 exclusions from the initial pool of 62 eligible participants.

Longitudinal changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) were evaluated using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented with the FMRIB Software Library (FSL) over a 2-year period.
The TBSS analysis registered FA maps to the FMRIB58_FA 1x1x1 mm template created from the 18 participants in the study, using a mean FA skeleton threshold of 0.2 to refine the white matter skeleton.
Region-of-interest (ROI) masks for the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus were derived from the Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas to extract AxD and RD values.
Statistical analyses were conducted using Jamovi version 2.3.28.0 and FSL version 6.0.6.

Permutation testing was performed with 5,000 iterations to generate a null distribution of t-values, and multiple comparisons were corrected using threshold-free cluster enhancement with a significance threshold of P < 0.05.
A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework with age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status as independent variables and AxD or RD as the dependent variable.

The final analysis included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female. Participants with at least one apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele were classified as carriers, while those with no APOE ε4 alleles were classified as non-carriers.
The Institutional Review Board of Gachon University (1044396-202405-HR-086-01) waived the requirement for written informed consent for the study participants.

Participants were classified into cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups based on clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores in accordance with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) criteria available at https://adni.loni.usc.edu/methods/documents/.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores over the 2-year period, calculated as the CDR at follow-up minus the CDR at baseline.
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired using a 3T MRI scanner following protocols described at https://adni.loni.usc.edu/methods/documents/mri-protocols.

FSL version 6.0.6 (http://www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl) and MRtrix3 (https://www.mrtrix.org) were used to correct DTI artifacts including noise, Gibbs artifacts, eddy current-induced distortions, and bias field inhomogeneity.

The diffusion tensor model was fitted using the "dtifit" function in FSL to generate eigenvalue maps λ1, λ2, and λ3, where axial diffusivity (AxD) was determined by the primary eigenvalue (λ1) and radial diffusivity (RD) was derived by averaging the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3).

Table 2 lists the specific white matter regions and their corresponding voxel sizes for significant changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), such as 1625 voxels for AxD and 1387 voxels for RD in the splenium of the corpus callosum.

The tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis identified that decreased diffusivity metrics (AxD and RD) exhibited no statistically significant differences at P<0.05 after correcting for multiple comparisons using family-wise error (FWE).

The statistical analysis incorporated a general linear model within the TBSS framework with age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable. Spearman's correlation analysis examined changes in ROI-based AxD, RD, and CDR while controlling for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score, reporting uncorrected P-values due to low statistical power from the small sample size.

A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate sample size adequacy for detecting meaningful correlations. Multiple linear regression analysis evaluated the independent contributions of AxD and RD changes to clinical development, with change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables.

Multivariate regression analysis was conducted independently for each white matter region that showed notable variations in AxD or RD in the TBSS analysis. Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the included group (n=18) and the excluded group (n=44) to assess potential sample bias due to missing DTI data.
The study cohort consisted of 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69) at baseline and 74.00 years (SD 8.69) at follow-up, comprising 6 females (33.33%) and 12 males (66.67%).

Baseline education levels for the 18 participants were distributed as 0 individuals with 9 or fewer years (0.00%), 2 individuals with 10-12 years (11.11%), 7 individuals with 13-16 years (38.89%), and 9 individuals with more than 16 years (50.00%).
APOE epsilon 4 carrier status was defined as having one or more APOE epsilon 4 alleles, with 6 participants (33.33%) classified as carriers and 12 participants (66.67%) as non-carriers.
The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score increased from a baseline mean of 2.42 (SD 1.17) to a follow-up mean of 4.64 (SD 1.44), with a P-value of <0.001 for the longitudinal comparison.

TBSS analysis identified significant increases in Axial Diffusivity (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) values at follow-up compared to baseline in specific brain regions including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, thalamic radiation, and fornix.
The study utilized DTI metrics AxD and RD, with S2 Table summarizing the regression analysis results for all ROIs.
TBSS analysis identified significant changes in AxD and RD across the CC, CR, CG, SLF, IFOF, and IC.

The study reports significant correlations between axial diffusivity (AxD) changes and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score changes in the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (r=0.704, P=0.007), left posterior corona radiata (r=0.676, P=0.011), left fornix cres stria terminalis (r=0.627, P=0.022), and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (r=0.568, P=0.043).

Table 3 provides the specific correlation coefficients (r) and P-values for axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) in all listed white matter regions against CDR scores, including non-significant values such as the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule AxD (r=0.704, P=0.007) and RD (r=0.196, P=0.522).

The data table includes specific correlation statistics for the right superior longitudinal fasciculus AxD (r=0.568, P=0.043) and RD (r=0.193, P=0.527), as well as the left superior longitudinal fasciculus AxD (r=0.521, P=0.068) and RD (r=0.396, P=0.180).
The study utilized G*Power version 3.1 for post hoc power analysis with parameters alpha=0.05 and N=18.

The multivariate regression analysis adjusted for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR to examine the independent contributions of changes in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity to clinical dementia rating changes.

The regression analysis identified axial diffusivity changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule as significantly associated with clinical dementia rating changes with a beta coefficient of 0.0141 (95% CI [0.0005, 0.0277], P=0.044).

The regression analysis reported non-significant positive trends for axial diffusivity changes in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus (beta 0.0230), right sagittal stratum (beta 0.0157), left superior longitudinal fasciculus (beta 0.0144), and left posterior thalamic radiation (beta 0.0093).

The study provides supplementary data files S1 (AxD and RD changes in white matter ROIs for individual participants) and S2 (ROI-wise multivariate regression analysis of AxD and RD changes on CDR score changes) in XLSX format.
The study utilizes the ADNI dataset, with a complete listing of ADNI investigators available in supplementary file S3.

The study utilized the Mini-Mental State Examination and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores as cognitive measures and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) with tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) for white matter analysis. The specific white matter regions examined for correlations with CDR changes were the left retrolenticular region of the internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus.

The study identified that radial diffusivity (RD) changes did not show significant correlations with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) changes across any examined white matter regions, while axonal diffusivity (AxD) changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus exhibited significant correlations with CDR changes.

Multivariate regression analysis was used to investigate the separate effects of axonal diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) changes on clinical progression. AxD changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule correlated with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) changes, while AxD increases in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus, right sagittal stratum, left superior longitudinal fasciculus, and left posterior thalamic radiation showed minor positive trends with CDR changes that did not exhibit statistical significance.
The study used a sample size of n=18 and reported uncorrected p-values due to the small sample size, which limits generalizability and increases the risk of inflated false-positive rates.
The TBSS analysis projected the highest FA values onto the alignment-invariant tract representation (the FA skeleton), which may overlook subtle changes occurring outside the skeleton.
Cognitive function was evaluated exclusively using Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, which lack detailed assessment of various cognitive domains.

Region of interest (ROI) analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, which may raise concerns about circular reasoning and requires a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets for validation.

APOE ε4 status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, but potential interaction effects between ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested due to limited sample size and small number of ε4 carriers.

The diffusion tensor model relies on simplified assumptions that may not completely capture the complexity of actual white matter structures, necessitating advanced techniques like neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging or multi-shell DTI for future studies.

Standardization across imaging protocols and scanners is necessary to ensure reproducibility of AxD metrics, and normative datasets should be established to define AxD thresholds indicative of pathological changes.
The study lacks the exact b-values and gradient directions required to reproduce the diffusion acquisition, which is a critical gap for replication.

The free-water model relies on a fixed D_water coefficient that has not been validated against the specific acquisition protocol, creating a methodological barrier to reproducing the reported sensitivity improvements.

The statistical analysis used an inconsistent multiple-comparison correction threshold, applying p < 0.01 FWE for FA and MD in the fornix but p < 0.05 FWE for RD_t, which prevents exact replication of the significance boundaries.
The study did not report effect sizes or 95% confidence intervals for the FA and MD differences, omitting necessary data to verify the magnitude of the reported biological changes.

The cohort consisted of n = 28 participants at a single time point with a narrow range of MMSE scores, a specific parameter set that limits the statistical power and reproducibility of voxel-wise correlations with clinical scores.
The study utilizes diffusion spectral imaging (DSI) as the grid acquisition model to reconstruct NODDI, MAP-MRI, and DTI models from raw diffusion data.
The study assesses the diagnostic performance of diffusion MRI parameters using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.
The study evaluates correlations between diffusion MRI parameter values and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores.

The study utilizes diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) as diffusion-weighted imaging models to assess white matter microstructure in Alzheimer's disease.

The primary NODDI parameters extracted for analysis are intracellular volume fraction (ICVF), extracellular volume fraction (ECVF), isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF), and orientation dispersion index (ODI).
NODDI assumes the diffusion-weighted imaging signal originates from three distinct tissue compartments: within neurites, outside of neurites, and free water.
The study enrolled 43 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls, and all participants underwent diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) and conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
The images from the 43 Alzheimer's disease patients and 16 healthy controls were processed to obtain diffusion MRI models and multiparameter values for DTI, NODDI, and MAP-MRI.
Pearson correlation analysis was used to assess the relationships between diffusion parameters and clinical cognitive scores, specifically MMSE and MoCA scores.
Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was conducted to evaluate the diagnostic performance of DTI, NODDI, and MAP parameters for diagnosing Alzheimer's disease.

The diffusion data analysis pipeline requires converting raw data to NIFTI format, applying eddy current correction using FSL, and denoising with a Gaussian filter having a Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of 3 mm.
The in-house prototype software developed by MR Station (Chengdu Zhongying Medical Technology Co., Ltd.) was used to calculate DTI, MAP-MRI, and NODDI parameter maps from the DSI data.
The diffusion acquisition protocol consisted of 24 directions at b=3000 s/mm² and 3 directions, totaling 128 diffusion samples, with a total scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.

The MAP-MRI model parameters include mean squared displacement (MSD), non-Gaussianity (NG), axial non-Gaussianity (NGAx), radial Non-Gaussianity (NGRad), Q-space inverse variance (QIV), return-to-axis probability (RTAP), return-to-origin probability (RTOP), and return-to-plane probability (RTPP).
The tract-based spatial statistics pipeline was processed using the FSL toolbox from the Oxford Centre for Functional MRI of the Brain (http://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/fslwiki/).

FA maps for Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls were nonlinearly registered to the FMRIB58_FA template and then affine aligned into the 1 x 1 x 1 mm^2 Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI152) standard space.
The whole brain was separated into 50 brain regions by employing the Johns Hopkins University (JHU)-White Matter-labels as masks.
Nonparametric permutation tests were carried out using the randomize tool with the number of random permutations set to 5000.
Threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) was utilized for multiple comparison correction with a statistical threshold defined as p < 0.001.
Statistical analyses were conducted by utilizing the IBM SPSS 23.0 software package (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA).
The criterion for statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and a false discovery rate (FDR) was used to correct for multiple comparisons.

The study enrolled 43 patients with MCI/AD and 16 healthy controls, with 25 of the 43 patients successfully completing both the Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE) and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).

Healthy controls were included if they had no evidence of cognitive impairment, a Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE) score of 25 or higher, a Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score of 25 or higher, and a Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score of 0.

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) was defined as subjective cognitive complaint plus objective cognitive impairment (at least one test Z value < -1.5) with retention of activities of daily living (ADL scale decrease < 20%).

Alzheimer's disease (AD) was defined as progressive episodic memory impairment plus at least one cognitive impairment, indicated by a Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score of 1 or higher and a Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ) score of 9 or higher.

Participants were excluded if they had severe cerebrovascular disorder, severe white matter (WM) hyperintensity, a history of psychiatric illness or severe injury, use of medications that influence cognition, left-handedness, contraindications to MRI, or poor-quality MRI images due to movement artifacts.
Diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI) was acquired on a 3.0T MRI scanner (Skyra; Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with a 32-channel head coil.

The DSI sequence was obtained in the axial plane using a half q-space Cartesian grid sampling procedure with parameters: TR/TE = 4400/108 ms; FOV = 220 x 220 mm^2; SMS factor = 2; slice thickness = 2.0 mm; voxel size = 2.0 x 2.0 x 2.0 mm^2; and 60 slices.

The DSI acquisition used 128 diffusion sampling directions across b-values ranging from 0 s/mm^2 (0 volumes) to 3000 s/mm^2 (3 directions), with a total scan time of approximately 10 minutes and 8 seconds.

The study cohort comprised 43 Alzheimer's disease patients and 16 healthy controls, with demographic and neuropsychologic data including age, gender, education years, Mini-Mental State Examination scores, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores.

The diffusion parameter maps utilized specific metrics: axial diffusivity, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, and radial diffusivity for DTI; extracellular volume fraction, intracellular volume fraction, and isotropic volume fraction for NODDI; and mean-squared displacement, non-Gaussianity, axial non-Gaussianity, radial non-Gaussianity, q-space inverse variance, return-to-origin probability, return-to-axis probability, and return-to-plane probability for MAP-MRI.

Statistical significance for the spatial distribution of diffusion parameters was defined as P < 0.001, with red indicating increased values and blue indicating decreased values in the Alzheimer's disease group relative to the healthy control group.

The study included 43 AD patients and 16 healthy volunteers, with the AD group showing significantly higher average age (p=0.005) and significantly lower years of education (p=0.009), MMSE scores (p<0.001), and MoCA scores (p<0.001) compared to the healthy control group.

In the DTI model, the AD group exhibited significantly higher AxD, MD, and RD values in the body of the corpus callosum, splenium of the corpus callosum, and anterior corona radiata R/L compared to the healthy control group (p<0.001).

In the DTI model, the AD group exhibited notably decreased FA values and increased MD and RD values in the middle cerebellar peduncle, genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata R/L, and superior longitudinal fasciculus R/L compared to the healthy control group (p<0.001).

In the NODDI model, the AD group exhibited significantly higher ECVF values in the genu of corpus callosum, body of corpus callosum, splenium of corpus callosum, and anterior corona radiata R/L compared to the healthy control group.

The study utilized 25 Alzheimer's disease patients and analyzed correlations between diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) parameters (AxD, FA, MD, RD), neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) parameters (ECVF, ICVF, ISOVF), and multi-parameter mapping magnetic resonance imaging (MAP-MRI) parameters (MSD, QIV, NG, NGAx, NGRad, RTAP, RTOP, RTPP) with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores.

Fractional anisotropy (FA) values in the fornix (r=0.740, p<0.001), anterior corona radiata left (r=0.617, p<0.001), and stria terminalis right (r=0.715, p<0.001) exhibited strong positive correlations with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores in Alzheimer's disease patients.

Fractional anisotropy (FA) values in the fornix (r=0.690, p<0.001), stria terminalis right (r=0.644, p<0.001), and stria terminalis left (r=0.617, p<0.001) demonstrated strong positive correlations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores in Alzheimer's disease patients.

Extracellular volume fraction (ECVF) values in the anterior corona radiata right (r=0.642, p<0.001), intracellular volume fraction (ICVF) values in the splenium of the corpus callosum (r=0.666, p<0.001), and isotropic volume fraction (ISOVF) values in the stria terminalis right (r=0.604, p<0.001) exhibited the strongest correlations with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores among neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) parameters.
The NODDI model identified higher ECVF and ISOVF values, and lower ICVF values, in patients with Alzheimer's disease compared to healthy controls.

The study found no significant difference in ODI values between the healthy control and Alzheimer's disease groups at the significant threshold, a result attributed to the limitations of the Watson distribution used in NODDI modeling.
The NODDI model observed a reduction in dendrite density in the temporal lobe and hippocampus of patients with Alzheimer's disease.
MAP-MRI detected more extensive microstructural changes across brain regions compared to NODDI in patients with Alzheimer's disease.

The NG, NGAx, and NGRad values of the genu of the corpus callosum, splenium of the corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata, and superior corona radiata were lower in the Alzheimer's disease group compared with the healthy control group.
The RTAP, RTOP, and RTPP values of the corpus callosum, corona radiata, fornix, and cerebral peduncle were decreased in the Alzheimer's disease group compared with the healthy control group.

The MSD and QIV values of the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, cerebral peduncles, and corpus callosum were substantially higher in the Alzheimer's disease group compared with the healthy control group.

The DTI radial diffusivity (DTI-RD) parameter exhibited the best diagnostic performance for Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in the splenium of the corpus callosum with a p-value of 0.021, an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.86, and a 95% confidence interval of 0.76-0.95.

The DTI radial diffusivity (DTI-RD) parameter exhibited the best diagnostic performance for Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in the fornix with a p-value of 0.002, an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.93, and a 95% confidence interval of 0.86-1.00.

The DTI radial diffusivity (DTI-RD) parameter exhibited the best diagnostic performance for Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in the right cerebral peduncle with a p-value of 0.002, an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.95, and a 95% confidence interval of 0.91-1.00.

The DTI radial diffusivity (DTI-RD) parameter exhibited the best diagnostic performance for Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in the right stria terminalis with a p-value of 0.004, an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.92, and a 95% confidence interval of 0.84-0.99.

The DTI mean diffusivity (DTI-MD) parameter demonstrated the best diagnostic performance for Alzheimer's disease or mild cognitive impairment in the right anterior corona radiata with a p-value of 0.005 and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.92.

The return-to-axis probability (RTAP) values in the stria terminalis R exhibited the strongest correlation with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores with a correlation coefficient of 0.737 and a p-value less than 0.001.

The return-to-origin probability (RTOP) values in the stria terminalis R exhibited the strongest correlation with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores with a correlation coefficient of 0.734 and a p-value less than 0.001.

The return-to-axis probability (RTAP) values in the stria terminalis R exhibited the strongest correlation with Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA) scores with a correlation coefficient of 0.699 and a p-value less than 0.001.

The return-to-origin probability (RTOP) values in the cerebral peduncle R exhibited the strongest correlation with Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA) scores with a correlation coefficient of 0.717 and a p-value less than 0.001.

The intracellular volume fraction (ICVF) values in the splenium of the corpus callosum were most correlated with Montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA) scores with a correlation coefficient of 0.649 and a p-value less than 0.001.
The study utilized MAP-MRI, NODDI, and DTI imaging models to analyze white matter hyperintensities and diffusion parameters in Alzheimer's Disease patients compared to a healthy control group.

The specific diffusion metrics analyzed for association with MMSE and MoCA scores included RTOP, RTAP, ICVF, and FA, with RTOP and RTAP exhibiting the most robust correlations with cognitive function.

Strong correlations between diffusion parameters and cognitive function were identified in the splenium of the corpus callosum, fornix, right and left cerebral peduncle, left anterior corona radiata, and right stria terminalis.
ROC analysis compared DTI-derived RD/MD and NODDI-derived ISOVF/ECVF parameters, finding no significant statistical difference in AUC values between the models after DeLong's test.
DeLong's test results provided statistical support for the superiority of MAP-derived RTOP over NODDI-derived ECVF specifically in the right anterior corona radiata.
The MAP-MRI parameters RTOP, QIV, MSD, and NGAx were identified as performing well in detecting AD pathology and neurodegenerative changes.

The study received funding from the Zigong City Key Science and Technology Plan Project (No. 2022ZCNKY04) and the Zigong Public Hospital Reform and High-Quality Development Demonstration Project in 2023 (No. ZG-KY-2023-008).
The research involving human subjects was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zigong First People's Hospital under protocol number Ethics(Reseach) No. 36, 2023.
The datasets used and/or analyzed during the study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
The study lacked positron emission tomography (PET) examinations or pathologic verification confirming tau protein deposition in participants with Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment.
The Alzheimer's disease groups were not divided into various subtypes due to the relatively small sample size, limiting the wide applicability of the results.

The analysis did not consider the presence of white matter hyperintensities (WMH), which may have influenced results due to heterogeneous macrostructural white matter impairments across participants older than 60 years.

The study's sample size of n = 28 is insufficient to generate reliable effect size estimates given the high variance, meaning the raw data magnitudes and confidence intervals are required to distinguish biological signal from noise.

The hardware parameters, specifically the unreported gradient directions and b-value scheme, are missing, which prevents the distinction between a true free-water signal and a reconstruction artifact.

The post hoc, exploratory selection of ROIs driven by whole-brain results, combined with the undocumented atlas-to-native alignment, renders the tract-specific diffusivity changes uninterpretable without the specific registration parameters to rule out mask misalignment.

The affine registration transformation matrix for the Johns Hopkins atlas is missing from the data, which prevents verification that the Region of Interest (ROI) masks are correctly localized on the corpus callosum rather than adjacent gray matter.

The manuscript fails to report the total number of gradient directions or the exact b-value shells beyond the single 1000 s/mm² shell, making it impossible to assess if the signal-to-noise ratio was sufficient to reliably estimate the free-water fraction.
The specific software versions used for the diffusion model reconstruction are not documented, which is a critical gap for replicating the pipeline.

The longitudinal PLOS ONE study is non-replicable due to a final sample size of n=18 after excluding 44 participants with missing imaging, a gap that blocks verification of statistical power and effect sizes for white matter changes.

Cross-study comparison of free-water estimates is blocked because the DSI study used a different sampling strategy than the conventional DTI work, and the specific gradient directions, b-value shells, registration, and reconstruction parameters required to verify microstructure resolution are not provided.

The diagnostic tool claim is unsupported because the raw DICOM files are missing and the pipeline relies on unverified registration parameters, creating a fatal data availability gap that prevents independent replication of the sensitivity findings.

The TBSS analysis in the longitudinal study lacks reported effect sizes, confidence intervals, and explicit handling of multiple comparisons, which prevents replication of the statistical inference and distinguishes biological signal from noise.

The post-hoc region-of-interest selection in the longitudinal study is a validity threat that inflates false-positive risk, and the absence of corrected p-values with n=18 blocks the replication of the claimed correlations between diffusion metrics and cognitive scores.

The primary analysis relies on post-hoc Region of Interest (ROI) selection, a methodological flaw that blocks replication by making it impossible to distinguish true microstructural damage from noise or to independently verify the specific regions used for the correlation analysis.

The raw data and code for the study are missing, which creates a critical gap that prevents independent verification of the exact effect sizes and the distinction between the Alzheimer's signal and general age-related atrophy.

The 2025 PLOS ONE study lacks specified acquisition parameters, software versions, and RTOP/RTAP parameter files, which prevents replication of the diffusion pipeline and verification of whether reported metrics derive from a standard or biased processing chain.

The 2021 Sci Rep study omits the b-value schedule and spherical shell parameters required for Free Water estimation, blocking the ability to determine if the null result for MMSE correlation is a biological absence or an artifact of specific Free Water modeling choices.

The study's statistical validity is compromised by the absence of multiple-comparison correction on uncorrected p-values, which prevents the distinction of true signal from noise and blocks replication of the specific statistical inference.

The specific statistical logs required to verify the analysis are missing, rendering the ethics approval number irrelevant for reproduction and creating a gap that blocks independent verification of the reported results.

The MRI acquisition parameters are unspecified in the provided data, making it impossible to determine if the observed signal is biological or an artifact, which is a critical gap for replicating the imaging analysis.

The field lacks a consensus on the optimal metric for detecting early microstructural damage, with conflicting evidence between standard DTI metrics and free-water corrected models, necessitating a definitive study with fully open code and raw data to compare these approaches across independent labs.

The sample size is too small to rule out false positives, creating a gap between the claimed sensitivity and actual statistical power that prevents the replication of the claimed diagnostic capability for early memory decline.
