documents: Prior diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) studies indicate that Alzheimer's disease is associated with lower fractional anisotropy and higher axial and radial diffusivity values in white matter regions such as the corpus callosum, fornix, cingulum, inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and superior longitudinal fasciculus. These white matter changes may precede neuronal loss and symptom onset, suggesting their potential utility as early biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

Although some studies report a correlation between DTI-derived metrics and cognitive scores, other investigations have failed to find a significant correlation, suggesting that methodological or analytic factors impact diffusion MRI data. The authors interpret these inconsistencies as potentially stemming from partial volume effects, where DTI metrics reflect a weighted average of multiple diffusion components rather than a single tissue type.

The study found that fractional anisotropy was decreased in Alzheimer's disease patients, primarily in the corpus callosum and fornix, which is consistent with known neurodegenerative mechanisms. Additionally, free-water diffusion tensor imaging revealed a significantly elevated free-water index in these regions, indicating that free water contributions impact standard diffusion tensor imaging metrics in neurodegenerative pathologies.

Free-water diffusion tensor imaging demonstrated improved consistency in fractional anisotropy, axial diffusivity, and radial diffusivity compared to standard diffusion tensor imaging. The authors interpret these results as evidence that free-water diffusion tensor imaging better reflects the underlying pathology of Alzheimer's disease and improves the accuracy of white matter integrity metrics.

Both standard and free-water diffusion tensor imaging showed higher values of mode of anisotropy coupled with higher fractional anisotropy in the anterior thalamic radiation and cortico-spinal tract of Alzheimer's disease patients. The authors attribute this finding most likely to a loss of crossing fibers in these white matter tracts.

Prior research established that DTI-based markers of altered microstructure are associated with CSF biomarkers of preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology, and that the Free Water index can serve as a standalone biomarker associated with cognitive decline.

The authors interpret that Free Water correction is particularly important in the fornix due to its anatomical proximity to the lateral ventricles and hippocampus, and may improve the sensitivity for detecting conversion to mild cognitive impairment compared to uncorrected metrics.

The study hypothesizes that removing Free Water contributions improves the accuracy of diffusion-derived metrics, thereby increasing the confidence in observed patterns and providing a clearer interpretation of white matter pathology in Alzheimer's disease.

The authors propose that quantifying Free Water yields complementary insight into sub-voxel white matter neurodegenerative processes, allowing for a better reflection of the underlying pathology in Alzheimer's disease.

The authors assert that applying FW-DTI for Alzheimer's disease better reflects the underlying pathology than standard methods, which should improve the interpretation of Alzheimer's disease white matter pathology.
The cognitively impaired group (AD only) showed significant differences in MMSE and CDR scores compared to the healthy control group, while no significant differences were found for age or sex.

The free-water (FW) model distinguishes between a tissue compartment and an isotropic free-water compartment, with the latter's diffusion coefficient set to the diffusivity of water at body temperature. Standard DTI metrics are reported as AxD, RD, and FA, while FW-corrected DTI metrics are reported as AxD_t, RD_t, and FA_t, where the subscript t indicates greater tissue specificity from FW-DTI.

The mode of anisotropy (MA) is a complementary measure to fractional anisotropy (FA) that discriminates between linear and planar anisotropy. MA is mathematically orthogonal to FA and relates to the skewness of the DTI eigenvalues.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects exhibited lower fractional anisotropy (FA) compared to healthy controls (HC) primarily in the fornix and corpus callosum, while small clusters in the right anterior thalamic radiation, cortical spinal tract, posterior limb of internal capsule, and superior corona radiata showed higher FA values in the AD group.

The AD group displayed more widespread differences in axial and radial diffusivity (AxD and RD) than in FA, with all significant clusters corresponding to higher AxD and RD values in AD and no clusters showing lower values.

Specific brain regions including the fornix, corpus callosum, forceps minor, and left cingulum showed a pattern where lower FA values overlapped with higher AxD and RD values between the AD and HC groups.

Higher FW index values in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) compared to healthy controls (HC) were observed widespread across cerebral white matter, covering 34% of the total white matter mask, with no significant clusters found where HC values were higher.

Significantly higher MA values in AD compared to HC were observed in the right CST, right PLIC, right SCR, and right SFOF, indicating more linear anisotropy, while lower MA values were found in the genu of CC and external capsule, indicating more planar anisotropy.

The study found significant differences in the Free Water index between Alzheimer's disease and healthy control groups, with only clusters showing higher Free Water values in Alzheimer's disease identified at a false discovery rate correction of p<0.01.

Significant differences between Alzheimer's disease and healthy control groups were localized to specific brain structures, including the anterior thalamic radiation, cingulum, corpus callosum, and internal capsule, for both standard and Free Water diffusion tensor imaging metrics.

In standard DTI analysis, only clusters with higher axial and radial diffusivities in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to healthy controls were found, with substantial overlap observed in the cingulum, fornix, and sagittal stratum.

Fractional anisotropy tensor analysis revealed that lower fractional anisotropy in the Alzheimer's disease group corresponded to the same white matter locations as standard fractional anisotry, specifically the fornix and corpus callosum, but covered smaller volumes of these structures.

Higher fractional anisotropy values in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to healthy controls were identified bilaterally in the anterior thalamic radiation, corticospinal tract, limb of the internal capsule, superior corona radiata, and superior fronto-occipital fasciculus.

Unlike standard DTI which only showed higher diffusivities, fractional anisotropy tensor analysis found both higher and lower axial and radial diffusivities in the Alzheimer's disease group, with lower axial diffusivity in the corpus callosum and fornix and higher axial diffusivity in the anterior thalamic radiation, corticospinal tract, and retrolenticular part of the internal capsule.

Lower radial diffusivity in the Alzheimer's disease group was observed in the anterior thalamic radiation, corticospinal tract, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and superior fronto-occipital fasciculus, which corresponded to areas showing higher fractional anisotropy.

In fractional anisotropy tensor analysis, no regions were observed where lower fractional anisotropy overlapped with higher axial and radial diffusivities, whereas lower fractional anisotropy overlapped with lower axial and radial diffusivities in the fornix and lower axial diffusivity in the corpus callosum and forceps minor.

Higher fractional anisotropy values overlapped with higher axial diffusivity and lower radial diffusivity in the superior fronto-occipital fasciculus, right posterior limb of the internal capsule, superior corona radiata, and anterior limb of the internal capsule.
Unlike standard DTI, no clusters in the fractional anisotropy tensor analysis demonstrated simultaneously higher axial and radial diffusivities in the Alzheimer's disease group.
No significant voxel-based correlation was found between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score and either standard or fiber-orientation-aware (FW) diffusion tensor imaging metrics.

Correlations between fractional anisotropy (FA) and diffusivity metrics increased substantially after FW correction, indicating that older healthy control participants have substantial fiber-orientation contributions to their dMRI-derived metrics.

The analysis found that fractional anisotropy (FW) values were significantly higher in the Alzheimer's disease group than in the healthy control group across various white matter tracts, including the anterior thalamic radiation, cortical spinal tract, and cingulum bundles. These significant differences were identified using both the JHU white matter tract atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white matter atlas.

The authors observed similar results for the mean anisotropy (MA) index using both standard DTI and FW-DTI analysis, with Figure 4 illustrating the clusters where MA was higher in the Alzheimer's disease group compared to the healthy control group.

Free water-corrected axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity metrics were more consistent with pathology-based expected spatial patterns of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease patients than standard metrics. The authors attribute this finding to the biophysical origin of these parameters, noting that raw diffusivity parameters are more impacted by intravoxel free-water diffusion than the composite fractional anisotropy metric.

The study found that the free water index was higher in Alzheimer's disease patients than in healthy controls across many regions, which was expected. Applying free water correction improved the accuracy and sensitivity of the resulting diffusion tensor imaging metrics, demonstrating the method's promise for neurological diseases with neurodegenerative aspects.

Removing the isotropic diffusion contribution via free water correction increases fractional anisotropy while decreasing axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity relative to standard diffusion tensor imaging metrics. Fractional anisotropy is less affected by the free water component than axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity, which is consistent with the widespread changes observed in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity without correction.

Free water (FW) correction revealed that lower fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum and fornix in Alzheimer's disease is driven by lower axial diffusivity, whereas standard DTI showed non-specific higher axial and radial diffusivity across white matter. This finding suggests that prior reports of higher axial diffusivity in Alzheimer's disease may have been artifacts of free water contamination rather than true pathology.

After free water correction, higher axial diffusivity was observed in regions with known crossing fibers, consistent with the degeneration of specific fiber tracts, while standard DTI failed to detect lower diffusivity values in Alzheimer's disease subjects.

The free water volume fraction was significantly higher in Alzheimer's disease patients across major white matter tracts, including the cingulum, inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and fornix, indicating a loss of white matter integrity. This free water index may serve as a valuable biomarker for sub-voxel neurodegenerative processes, as previous studies linked higher free water values to poorer executive and visuomotor performance.

No significant voxel-wise correlations were found between Mini-Mental State Examination scores and DTI metrics in the Alzheimer's disease cohort, likely due to the narrow range of cognitive scores in this predominantly mild patient group. The authors suggest that implementing free water correction is a methodological improvement for future studies aiming to correlate white matter integrity with cognitive function, particularly for axial and radial diffusivity metrics.

The application of free-water (FW) correction in Alzheimer's disease (AD) improves the accuracy and sensitivity of diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics, confirming that lower fractional anisotropy (FA) in the fornix reflects true pathological changes rather than partial volume effects from atrophy or ventricular expansion.

Lower FA and higher mean diffusivity (MD) in the fornix are consistent with neurodegenerative changes and prior findings linking these metrics to early-stage AD and cognitive decline, with the fornix being a major output tract of the hippocampus critical for episodic memory.

FW-corrected DTI revealed large clusters of lower FA in the genu and body of the corpus callosum (CC) with minimal splenial changes, a pattern that supports the anterior-to-posterior progression of the retrogenesis hypothesis over the posterior-to-anterior pattern of Wallerian degeneration.

The observation of higher FA in the anterior thalamic radiation (ATR), corticospinal tract (CST), and other regions in AD using FW-DTI is interpreted as the loss of crossing fibers rather than true microstructural preservation, a phenomenon obscured by standard DTI's inability to resolve multi-directional fiber orientations.

Higher mean anisotropy (MA) in AD subjects within the right CST, posterior limb of the internal capsule (PLIC), and superior corona radiata (SCR) corroborates the presence of fiber crossing and suggests degeneration of fiber tracts in the ATR, CC, and fasciculus, consistent with prior studies reporting parallel increases of FA and MA in these areas.

The study demonstrates that implementing a Free Water (FW) correction algorithm for Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) improves the sensitivity and specificity of derived metrics by removing partial volume effects, allowing for a better capture of underlying Alzheimer's disease-related pathologic changes compared to standard DTI approaches.

While significantly altered DTI metrics were found in Alzheimer's disease compared to healthy controls for both standard and FW-DTI, the FW-DTI identified changes were more consistent with known Alzheimer's disease pathology in terms of the magnitude and direction of the changes.

The Free Water (FW) index may improve sensitivity to sub-voxel neurodegeneration, while the Mean Apparent (MA) metric may improve specificity related to crossing fibers, thereby enhancing the reliability and inter-parameter consistency of DTI metrics in the presence of atrophy.

No significant voxel-based correlations were observed between standard DTI and FW-DTI metrics and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score, a finding consistent with previous studies that suggests the relationship between global cognitive scores and white matter pathology in Alzheimer's disease may not be linear.

The study's primary finding is that standard brain scans underestimate the extent of damage in individuals with early memory loss, while a newer, more precise imaging method reveals that the pathology is likely more widespread than previously thought. This interpretation suggests that current diagnostic tools may miss significant structural changes, though the authors caution that this finding does not allow for predicting the specific rate of disease progression for any individual patient.

The study found significant longitudinal increases in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) over two years in widespread white matter tracts, including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, cingulum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and fornix, in patients transitioning from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease.

Changes in axial diffusivity (AxD), particularly in the left retrolenticular internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus, showed significant correlations with cognitive decline, whereas radial diffusivity (RD) changes were not significantly associated with clinical dementia rating score changes in any region.

Multivariate regression analysis identified axial diffusivity (AxD) in the left retrolenticular internal capsule as a significant independent predictor of cognitive decline, leading the authors to interpret AxD as a sensitive biomarker for microstructural white matter alterations and early detection during the transition from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease.

Participants were classified into cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease groups based on clinical dementia rating scores, with cognitive decline defined as the change in these scores over a 2-year period.

xD was sensitive to microstructural alterations in white matter associated with cognitive decline during the transition from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease, suggesting it may serve as a valuable biomarker for early detection and monitoring of Alzheimer's disease progression.

Previous magnetic resonance imaging studies have highlighted substantial microstructural damage in the white matter, but whether white matter damage is an early pathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease remains unclear.

Diffusion tensor imaging can detect microstructural changes and the integrity of white matter tracts in specific brain regions, addressing the limitations of structural MRI in detecting subtle white matter damage in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease.

The study hypothesized that white matter damage, indicated by increased Axonal Damage (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) values, represents early pathological changes such as axonal degeneration and demyelination during the progression from Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's Disease (AD).
The study hypothesized that white matter damage, as assessed by changes in Axonal Damage (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD), is associated with cognitive decline.

Longitudinal analyses of Axonal Damage (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) over time can elucidate the progression of white matter damage and its causal relationship with cognitive decline, potentially establishing white matter damage as an early marker of Alzheimer's Disease (AD).

The authors noted that the cross-sectional design of most previous studies limited their ability to capture the dynamic nature of white matter changes over time, highlighting the need for longitudinal studies to evaluate early detection and timely intervention.
The study found a statistically significant increase in the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score over two years, indicating substantial cognitive decline in the participants.

The authors confirmed that excluding participants with missing DTI data did not introduce sample bias, as no significant differences were found in age, sex, education level, APOE epsilon 4 carrier status, or baseline CDR between the included and excluded groups.

TBSS analysis revealed a significant increase in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) values at the follow-up examination compared to baseline across extensive brain regions, including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, and thalamic radiation.

The study found that the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score significantly increased from a baseline mean of 2.42 to a follow-up mean of 4.64, indicating a progression in dementia severity over the study period.

Axial diffusivity (AxD) changes exhibited the strongest correlation with changes in the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score, with significant associations found in the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus.

The study found that axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) values in the corpus callosum exhibited extensive changes, with the largest increases in AxD occurring in the superior longitudinal fasciculus and posterior corona radiata. Widespread increases in these metrics were also observed in the internal capsule, corona radiata, and cingulum cingulate gyrus, indicating considerable white matter microstructural changes over the two-year follow-up period.

Tract-based spatial statistics revealed significant increases in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity at baseline and follow-up, with the most pronounced changes localized to the splenium of the corpus callosum, anterior and superior corona radiata, and the superior longitudinal fasciculus.

AxD changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule were significantly associated with CDR changes in a multivariate regression analysis adjusting for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR. AxD changes in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus, right sagittal stratum, left superior longitudinal fasciculus, and left posterior thalamic radiation exhibited weak positive trends with CDR changes, although these associations were not statistically significant.
No significant correlations were observed between the changes in radial diffusivity and changes in CDR scores across any of the examined white matter regions.

Partial correlation plots demonstrated the association between AxD change and CDR change in four significant white matter regions: the left retrolenticular internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix crossing stria terminalis, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus.

Tract-based spatial statistics analysis revealed a significant increase in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity in the corpus callosum, cingulum, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, with the widespread increase in axial diffusivity correlating with cognitive decline. In contrast, changes in radial diffusivity across all examined white matter regions did not significantly associate with Clinical Dementia Rating changes, indicating that axial diffusivity is more closely related to cognitive decline.

The authors interpret the observed white matter damage in the corpus callosum, cingulum, and superior longitudinal fasciculus as a vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease that leads to cognitive and functional impairments by disrupting interhemispheric communication, limbic system connections, and motor coordination. These findings suggest that the structural degradation of these specific tracts is a mechanism underlying the observed deficits in memory, attention, and language processing.

The study's findings align with prior cross-sectional and longitudinal research that reported increased axial and radial diffusivity in the corpus callosum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and cingulum in patients with Alzheimer's disease and during the progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease. The authors note that previous studies have also established significant correlations between cognitive scores and diffusivity changes in the posterior cingulum, supporting the link between white matter structural changes and cognitive performance.

Axonal degeneration in the left retrolenticular region of the internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus correlates with cognitive decline, a finding consistent with prior research linking these specific pathways to memory and executive function.

The study found no significant correlation between radial diffusivity changes and cognitive decline, suggesting that axonal degeneration rather than myelin loss is the predominant driver of clinical progression at this disease stage.

The authors interpret the lack of radial diffusivity associations as a temporal dynamic where demyelination follows earlier axonal damage, and they conclude that axonal diffusivity is a sensitive indicator of early pathological changes in Alzheimer's disease.

Multivariate regression analysis confirmed that axonal diffusivity changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule independently correlate with cognitive decline, while increases in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus and other regions showed minor positive trends that did not reach statistical significance.

Axonal damage (AxD) changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule serve as independent predictors of cognitive decline, reinforcing the hypothesis that axonal damage is the primary driver of microstructural alterations in Alzheimer's disease progression.

The authors interpret the lack of significant association between radial diffusivity (RD) and cognitive decline to mean that myelin loss is not the primary driver of disease progression, whereas AxD is a reliable marker for identifying and monitoring the initial progression of Alzheimer's disease.

The longitudinal analysis of progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease provides a clearer understanding of the temporal progression of white matter integrity changes and their association with cognitive decline, offering advantages over previous cross-sectional studies.

The authors note that inconsistent reporting of AxD changes across prior studies may be attributed to multiple pathological processes, including axonal damage, inflammatory responses, and changes in the extracellular space, which complicates the interpretation of AxD as a specific indicator of pathology.

A significant correlation was observed between white matter microstructural changes, specifically axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), and cognitive decline during the progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease. The authors interpret an increase in AxD as a sensitive indicator of early pathological changes and a potential biomarker for early detection and monitoring of Alzheimer's disease progression.

The study found that an increase in radial diffusivity (RD) was observed in fewer brain regions compared to axial diffusivity, highlighting the distinct roles of white matter diffusion metrics in reflecting axonal versus myelin pathology.

The claim that the new scan metrics better reflect underlying disease is unsupported because the free-water model's sensitivity to noise is unverified; without longitudinal data or a larger cohort to rule out that the 'extra damage' is merely an amplification of noise by the unvalidated model parameters, the observed differences cannot be distinguished from methodological artifacts.

The study found that diffusion metrics RTOP, RTAP, ICVF, and FA were most strongly related to MMSE and MoCA cognitive scores, with RTOP and RTAP exhibiting the strongest relationship to cognitive function.

The authors interpret the findings to mean that DTI, NODDI, and MAP-MRI diffusion models are all suitable markers for studying Alzheimer's disease, with detailed parameters providing more information about the brain's microstructural changes in patients.

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is identified as a prodromal stage of Alzheimer's disease (AD), supported by neuropathological studies showing that over 80% of amnestic MCI patients exhibit AD-type biomarkers (Aβ+/tau+).

The authors interpret neurodegeneration, specifically synapse and neuron loss and myelin degradation, as the most direct pathological substrate of clinical symptoms in AD, noting that these changes precede volumetric changes.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is the most widely used diffusion-weighted imaging model for studying white matter changes in AD, but it has a known limitation where the assumption of Gaussian water diffusion weakens its capability to detect diffusion heterogeneity in brain tissue.

Neurite Orientation Density and Dispersion Imaging (NODDI) is interpreted as superior to DTI in evaluating neurodegeneration and the pathological biology of AD because it characterizes brain changes in specific microstructural environments by assuming the signal emanates from three distinct tissue compartments: within neurites, outside of neurites, and free water.

MAP-MRI characterizes the full probability density function of water molecular displacements using orthogonal Hermite basis functions, which enables the resolution of complex microstructure features beyond the Gaussian diffusion assumption of DTI.

Prior MAP-MRI studies found that white matter microstructure degeneration occurs earlier than macroscopic structural changes during aging and that reduced white matter fiber complexity is directly associated with neurocognitive aging.

Existing research on Alzheimer's disease has primarily focused on DTI and NODDI models, leaving the application of MAP-MRI and its correlation with cognitive function in Alzheimer's disease unexplored.
The study aims to reveal specific microstructure damage patterns of Alzheimer's disease and their association with cognitive decline by combining NODDI, MAP-MRI, and DTI.

The study assesses the diagnostic performance of different diffusion MRI parameters for detecting Alzheimer's disease-related white matter damage and evaluates their correlations with Mini-Mental State Examination and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores.

Using diffusion spectral imaging allows for the concurrent acquisition of multiple diffusion MRI models from raw data, which saves time and cost while enabling comparative assessment to identify subtleties in brain microstructure.
The study enrolled 43 patients diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment or dementia due to probable Alzheimer's disease and 16 healthy controls for a primary analysis.

The diagnosis of cognitive impairment, including mild cognitive impairment or dementia due to probable Alzheimer's disease, was established based on clinical and cognitive information according to the 2011 National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association diagnostic criteria.

In the DTI model, the Alzheimer's disease group exhibited significantly higher axial diffusivity, mean diffusivity, and radial diffusivity values, along with notably decreased fractional anisotropy values, in specific brain regions including the corpus callosum, anterior corona radiata, middle cerebellar peduncle, and superior longitudinal fasciculus compared to the healthy control group.

In the NODDI model, the Alzheimer's disease group showed significantly higher extracellular volume fraction values in the genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum and the anterior corona radiata compared to the healthy control group.

The ICVF values in the splenium of the corpus callosum showed the strongest correlation with MoCA scores among the evaluated diffusion parameters, while ECVF, ODI, and ISOVF values for any fiber did not show significant correlations with MoCA scores.

For MAP-derived parameters, RTAP values in the stria terminalis R and RTOP values in the cerebral peduncle R exhibited the strongest correlations with MoCA scores, whereas RTAP and RTOP values in the stria terminalis R showed the strongest correlations with MMSE scores.

The DTI radial diffusivity parameter exhibited the best diagnostic performance for distinguishing AD or MCI in the splenium of the corpus callosum, fornix, right cerebral peduncle, left cerebral peduncle, and right stria terminalis, while the DTI mean diffusivity parameter demonstrated the best performance in the right anterior corona radiata.

In the Alzheimer's disease group, extracellular volume fraction values were significantly higher than in the healthy control group, primarily within the genu, body, and splenium of the corpus callosum, as well as the anterior and superior corona radiata. The authors indicate that these specific brain regions exhibit distinct microstructural changes associated with the disease.

Compared to healthy controls, the Alzheimer's disease group showed increased extracellular volume fraction, intracellular volume fraction, mean-squared displacement, and q-space inverse variance values in specific regions including the corpus callosum, frontal lobe, and cerebral peduncle. Conversely, the Alzheimer's disease group exhibited decreased radial non-Gaussianity, return-to-axis probability, return-to-origin probability, and return-to-plane probability values in the corpus callosum and corona radiata regions.

In Alzheimer's disease patients, fractional anisotropy (FA) values in the fornix, anterior corona radiata left, and stria terminalis right showed strong positive correlations with Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores, while FA values in the fornix and stria terminalis (right and left) correlated strongly with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores.

Among diffusion tensor imaging parameters, fractional anisotropy values demonstrated significantly stronger correlations with cognitive scale scores than axial diffusivity, mean diffusivity, or radial diffusivity, which exhibited negative correlations with cognitive performance.

Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) parameters, specifically extracellular volume fraction in the anterior corona radiata right, intracellular volume fraction in the splenium of corpus callosum, and isotropic volume fraction in the stria terminalis right, exhibited the strongest correlations with MMSE scores.

The study found that white matter microstructural changes in Alzheimer's disease patients are significant and potentially more widespread than typically recognized, which may provide insights into alternative pathological mechanisms contributing to dementia.
The authors interpret that DTI, NODDI, and MAP-MRI are clinically viable tools for identifying microstructural changes associated with Alzheimer's disease and reflecting clinical cognitive status.
MAP-MRI parameters are interpreted as more directly correlating with brain tissue microstructure and characterizing non-Gaussian diffusion profiles that reflect complex tissue organization.

The study concludes that DTI, NODDI, and MAP models are all effective markers for studying Alzheimer's disease, with different parameters offering valuable insights into brain microstructural changes in patients.

White matter changes in Alzheimer's disease are more widespread than previously recognized, extending to the brain stem and cerebellum hemispheres, which aligns with prior findings and suggests these whole-brain alterations play a vital role in the clinical manifestation of the disease.

MAP-MRI parameters, particularly RTOP and RTAP, outperformed NODDI and DTI parameters in their association with cognitive function, indicating that reductions in these metrics reflect axonal degeneration, demyelination, and neuronal loss in Alzheimer's disease pathology.

Strong correlations between diffusion parameters and cognitive function were observed in the splenium of the corpus callosum, fornix, cerebral peduncle, anterior corona radiata, and stria terminalis, which are consistent with previous studies and highlight the importance of limbic and interhemispheric tracts in cognitive pathways.

The NODDI model was found to be non-inferior to the DTI model in diagnostic accuracy, providing complementary insights into neurite density and orientation dispersion that augment the findings of DTI and MAP-MRI.

MAP-MRI parameters such as RTOP, QIV, MSD, and NGAx performed well in detecting Alzheimer's disease pathology, a result consistent with prior work and attributed to their ability to characterize non-Gaussian diffusion profiles that reflect complex tissue organization.

MAP-MRI metrics such as NG, RTAP, RTOP, and RTPP showed significant changes in the corpus callosum and corona radiata of Alzheimer's disease patients, which the authors interpret as indicators of reduced tissue complexity, axonal swelling, and impaired fiber integrity. These findings suggest that MAP-MRI is sensitive to the microstructural signatures of Alzheimer's-related neurodegeneration.

NODDI analysis revealed higher extracellular volume fraction and lower intracellular volume fraction in Alzheimer's disease patients, which the authors attribute to extracellular amyloid accumulation and tau protein tangles that physically constrain intracellular space. This interpretation links the diffusion changes to the physical disruption of axonal integrity and the expansion of the extracellular matrix.

The lack of significant difference in the orientation dispersion index between healthy controls and Alzheimer's disease patients is interpreted as resulting from the limitations of the Watson distribution in NODDI modeling when applied to complex tissue structures. The authors suggest that bidirectional pathological effects, such as dendritic pruning and neurite beading, may cancel each other out in heterogeneous subregions, leading to nonsignificant group differences.

MAP-MRI detected more extensive microstructural changes across brain regions compared to NODDI, a finding consistent with previous studies and attributed to MAP-MRI's ability to characterize non-Gaussian diffusion profiles that reflect complex tissue organization. The authors conclude that parameters from different imaging models capture different dimensions of the pathological process, thereby complementing the understanding of Alzheimer's disease mechanisms.

The study's use of the Johns Hopkins tractography atlas to define regions of interest for the corpus callosum, cingulum, and uncinate fasciculus is problematic because the manuscript does not specify how the atlas was spatially normalized to the cohort's native space, a registration step that could misalign masks and bias extracted diffusivity values.

The study's failure to report the specific b-value scheme and gradient directions prevents researchers from distinguishing a true free-water signal from a reconstruction artifact, undermining the validity of the reported diffusion metrics.

The omission of the total number of gradient directions and specific b-value shells beyond the single 1000 s/mm² shell in the manuscript creates a critical bottleneck, making it impossible to determine if the signal-to-noise ratio was sufficient to reliably estimate the free-water fraction.

The longitudinal PLOS ONE study effectively tested only 18 participants after excluding 44 with missing imaging, a sample size too small to distinguish true white matter microstructural changes from noise. This statistical limitation undermines the authors' interpretation that the metrics offer superior sensitivity, as the data cannot support claims of specific biological signal over general age-related atrophy.

Cross-paper synthesis is invalid because the DSI study used a fundamentally different sampling strategy than the conventional DTI work, making free-water estimates directly incomparable without verified gradient directions and b-value shells. The authors' interpretation of consistent microstructural changes across cohorts is an unstable foundation, as the inconsistent acquisition protocols prevent distinguishing true biological signals from fitting artifacts.

The claim that the technique improves sensitivity is not a supported finding but a hope based on a pipeline with unverified registration and unavailable raw DICOM files. This represents a failure of basic scientific hygiene rather than a mere limitation, as the missing data makes it impossible to verify the reliability of the diagnostic tool or the accuracy of the ROI masks on the correct tissue.

The post-hoc selection of regions of interest in the PLOS ONE study creates a fatal validity threat that prevents the distinction between true microstructural damage and statistical noise, particularly given the small sample size of n=18 and the absence of multiple-comparison corrections.

The inability to independently verify the analytical pipelines of the Sci Rep and PLOS ONE studies stems from the missing raw diffusion data, code, and specific software versions, which means the reported findings could be computational artifacts rather than true biological signals.

The claim that diffusion metrics capture damage before neuronal loss is unsupported because the primary analysis relies on circular ROI selection, and the signal has not been distinguished from general aging or comorbid vascular pathology.

The null result in the 2021 Sci Rep study regarding Free Water estimation cannot be interpreted as a true biological absence of correlation because the missing b-value schedule and spherical shell parameters prevent verification of whether the outcome is an artifact of specific Free Water modeling choices.

The primary validity threat in the current analysis is the lack of multiple-comparison correction on an uncorrected p-value basis, which prevents researchers from distinguishing true signal from noise in the data.

The correlation between white matter changes and symptoms in the study rests on a sample size too small to rule out false positives, leaving a gap between the claimed sensitivity and the actual statistical power of the cohort.
Unspecified acquisition parameters in the imaging study prevent the determination of whether the observed signal is biological or an artifact, meaning the scan is not ready for clinical use.
